cards.q: Which part of the eye does most of the bending of incoming light?
cards.a: The cornea.
options: The vitreous humor
The lens
The cornea
The aqueous humor
cards.explanation: Light passes from air into the cornea, and that is the largest jump in refractive index anywhere in the eye, so the cornea supplies roughly two thirds of the total refractive power. The lens supplies the rest, and it matters because it is the part that can change shape, but its power is smaller. The vitreous humor and the aqueous humor have refractive indexes close to the tissues around them, so light passes through them with very little bending.

cards.q: Which muscle contracts so that the lens can round up for near vision?
cards.a: The ciliary muscle.
options: The ciliary muscle
The sphincter pupillae
The dilator pupillae
The levator palpebrae superioris
cards.explanation: The ciliary muscle is a ring of smooth muscle, and when it contracts the ring narrows, which slackens the zonular fibers and lets the elastic lens spring into a rounder shape. The sphincter pupillae narrows the pupil during the near response but does not change lens shape. The dilator pupillae widens the pupil under sympathetic drive. The levator palpebrae raises the eyelid and has nothing to do with focusing.

cards.q: During accommodation for a near object, how does the lens change?
cards.a: It becomes more rounded and gains refractive power.
options: It flattens and loses refractive power
It becomes more rounded and gains refractive power
It slides backward toward the retina
It stays the same shape while the cornea steepens
cards.explanation: A rounder lens has more sharply curved surfaces, so it bends light more strongly, which is exactly what the diverging rays from a near object need. Flattening is what happens for distance vision, when the ciliary muscle relaxes. The human lens does not move forward or backward to focus, unlike a camera lens. The cornea has a fixed curvature and does not participate in accommodation.

cards.q: Which cranial nerve carries the parasympathetic fibers that drive accommodation and pupillary constriction?
cards.a: The oculomotor nerve, CN III.
options: The oculomotor nerve, CN III
The trochlear nerve, CN IV
The abducens nerve, CN VI
The optic nerve, CN II
cards.explanation: Parasympathetic fibers travel with CN III, synapse in the ciliary ganglion, and innervate both the ciliary muscle and the sphincter pupillae. CN II is purely sensory and carries the incoming light signal, so it is the afferent limb rather than the motor output. CN IV and CN VI each move one extraocular muscle and carry no parasympathetic fibers to the inside of the eye.

cards.q: Which autonomic division constricts the pupil, and which muscle does it act on?
cards.a: Parasympathetic, acting on the circular sphincter muscle.
options: Sympathetic, acting on the radial dilator muscle
Parasympathetic, acting on the circular sphincter muscle
Sympathetic, acting on the ciliary muscle
Parasympathetic, acting on the radial dilator muscle
cards.explanation: The iris has two muscle layers with opposite geometry, and the circular sphincter is the parasympathetic one, so when it shortens the pupil narrows. The sympathetic division acts on the radial dilator, whose fibers run like spokes, so shortening them pulls the pupil open. The ciliary muscle is parasympathetic but it shapes the lens rather than the pupil, and no autonomic division pairs the parasympathetic supply with the radial muscle.

cards.q: What is the afferent limb of the pupillary light reflex?
cards.a: The optic nerve.
options: The oculomotor nerve
The trigeminal nerve
The ciliary ganglion
The optic nerve
cards.explanation: Light striking the retina is signaled to the midbrain over ganglion cell axons in the optic nerve, so CN II is the sensory arm of the reflex. The oculomotor nerve is the motor arm that carries the constriction command back to the iris. The trigeminal nerve carries corneal sensation, which drives the blink reflex rather than the light reflex. The ciliary ganglion sits on the motor side, where the preganglionic parasympathetic fibers synapse.

cards.q: Which three changes make up the near response?
cards.a: Accommodation, convergence, and pupillary constriction.
options: Accommodation, convergence, and corneal flattening
Accommodation, divergence, and pupillary dilation
Corneal steepening, convergence, and pupillary dilation
Accommodation, convergence, and pupillary constriction
cards.explanation: Looking at something close requires more lens power, both eyes turned inward so the images land on corresponding retinal points, and a smaller pupil to sharpen the image. Divergence and pupillary dilation belong to the shift back toward distance viewing. The cornea does not change curvature in either direction, so any option built on corneal steepening or flattening describes something the eye cannot do.

cards.q: What unit expresses the refractive power of a lens?
cards.a: The diopter.
options: The lumen
The millimeter of mercury
The decibel
The diopter
cards.explanation: Refractive power in diopters is the reciprocal of the focal length in meters, so a lens that focuses at 0.5 m has a power of 2 diopters. The lumen measures light output, which is about the source rather than the bending of rays. Millimeters of mercury measure pressure, including intraocular pressure, and decibels measure sound intensity.

cards.q: A student looks up from a distant clock to a book held 25 cm away. What happens to the tension on the zonular fibers?
cards.a: It falls, because the ciliary muscle contracts and the ciliary ring narrows.
options: It rises, because the ciliary muscle relaxes and the ciliary ring widens
It rises, because the ciliary muscle contracts and pulls the fibers tight
It does not change, because the zonular fibers are rigid
It falls, because the ciliary muscle contracts and the ciliary ring narrows
cards.explanation: The ciliary muscle is arranged as a ring around the lens, so contraction makes the ring smaller and moves the attachment points closer to the lens, which slackens the zonules and lets the lens round up. Rising tension with a relaxing muscle describes what happens on the way back to distance viewing. The idea that contraction tightens the fibers is the most common error here, because it assumes a muscle pulling on a rope rather than a sphincter closing down. The zonules are flexible and their tension changes constantly.

cards.q: A light is shone into the right eye only. What happens to the left pupil?
cards.a: It constricts, because of the consensual reflex.
options: It constricts, because of the consensual reflex
It dilates, because that eye is still in relative darkness
It does not change, because each optic nerve drives only its own eye
It constricts only if the light is moved to the left eye as well
cards.explanation: Signals from one optic nerve reach the pretectal area and then both Edinger-Westphal nuclei, so a light in one eye constricts both pupils. That crossed connection is the whole point of testing the direct and consensual responses separately. The idea that each eye works alone would predict no consensual response at all, and dilation of the unlit eye would require sympathetic drive that the reflex does not produce.

cards.q: Eye drops that block muscarinic receptors are placed in one eye. What happens to near vision in that eye?
cards.a: Near vision blurs, because the ciliary muscle cannot contract.
options: Near vision blurs, because the ciliary muscle cannot contract
Near vision is unchanged, because accommodation is sympathetic
Near vision sharpens, because the lens rounds up further
Distance vision blurs, because the lens is locked in a rounded shape
cards.explanation: Ciliary muscle contraction depends on acetylcholine acting at muscarinic receptors, so blocking those receptors leaves the muscle relaxed, the zonules taut, and the lens flat. A flat lens is set for distance, so far vision stays clear while near vision goes soft. Accommodation is parasympathetic, not sympathetic, and a lens locked in the rounded shape would be the result of a muscarinic agonist instead.

cards.q: In dim light the pupil dilates. What happens to the depth of focus?
cards.a: It decreases, because a wide pupil admits more peripheral rays.
options: It decreases, because a wide pupil admits more peripheral rays
It increases, because a wide pupil narrows the cone of light entering the eye
It is unchanged, because depth of focus depends only on lens power
It increases, because more light reaching the retina sharpens the image
cards.explanation: A wide pupil lets in rays that strike the lens far from its center, and those rays converge over a wider spread of distances, so only a narrow band of object distances stays sharp. A small pupil does the opposite and acts like the small aperture on a camera. Total light and lens power both change the image, but neither one is what sets depth of focus, which is governed by aperture size.

cards.q: A surgeon flattens the central cornea. What happens to the refractive power of the eye and to the focal point?
cards.a: Power falls and the focal point moves backward, toward the retina.
options: Power falls and the focal point moves forward, in front of the retina
Power rises and the focal point moves forward, away from the retina
Power falls and the focal point moves backward, toward the retina
Power rises and the focal point moves backward, behind the retina
cards.explanation: A flatter surface bends light less, so refractive power drops and the rays converge farther back inside the eye. That is why flattening the cornea corrects myopia, where the image was landing in front of the retina. The pairings that raise power with a backward shift, or lower power with a forward shift, reverse the relationship between power and focal length, which are inversely related.

cards.q: A frightened person's pupils widen. Which muscle and which transmitter produced this?
cards.a: The radial dilator pupillae, with norepinephrine acting on alpha receptors.
options: The circular sphincter pupillae, with acetylcholine on muscarinic receptors
The ciliary muscle, with acetylcholine on muscarinic receptors
The radial dilator pupillae, with norepinephrine on alpha receptors
The circular sphincter pupillae, with norepinephrine on alpha receptors
cards.explanation: Fear raises sympathetic outflow, and sympathetic postganglionic fibers release norepinephrine onto alpha receptors of the radial dilator muscle, which pulls the pupil open. Acetylcholine on the sphincter would narrow the pupil instead. Acetylcholine on the ciliary muscle changes lens shape rather than pupil size. Pairing norepinephrine with the sphincter mixes the transmitter of one pathway with the muscle of the other.

cards.q: An object is moved from 6 m away to 30 cm away. What must happen to the refractive power of the eye for the image to stay on the retina?
cards.a: It must rise, because rays from a near object arrive diverging.
options: It must fall, because near objects need less bending
It must stay the same, because the cornea does all of the focusing
It must rise, because rays from a near object arrive diverging
It must fall, because the eyeball lengthens during near work
cards.explanation: Rays from a distant object arrive nearly parallel, but rays from a near object are still spreading when they reach the eye, so more bending is needed to bring them to a point on the retina. That extra power comes from the lens rounding up. The cornea does most of the baseline focusing but cannot change, and the eyeball does not change length from moment to moment.

cards.q: A swimmer with normal eyes opens them underwater without goggles and everything looks badly blurred. What explains this?
cards.a: Water and cornea have almost the same refractive index, so the cornea loses its power.
options: Water and cornea have almost the same refractive index, so the cornea loses its power
Water keeps the ciliary muscle from contracting, so accommodation fails
Water raises corneal refractive power beyond what the lens can offset
Water clouds the aqueous humor and scatters the light before it reaches the photoreceptors
cards.explanation: Bending happens at an interface only when the two media differ in refractive index, and water is close enough to corneal tissue that the largest refracting surface in the eye stops working. The lens alone cannot supply the missing two thirds of the power, so images focus far behind the retina. Goggles restore an air interface in front of the cornea, which is why they fix the problem instantly. Water does not touch ciliary muscle function or the clarity of the aqueous humor, which sits behind the cornea.

cards.q: Shining a light in the right eye constricts both pupils. Shining the same light in the left eye constricts neither pupil. Where is the lesion?
cards.a: The left optic nerve, the afferent limb from that eye.
options: The left optic nerve, the afferent limb from that eye
The left oculomotor nerve, the efferent limb to that eye
The right optic nerve, the afferent limb from that eye
The right oculomotor nerve, the efferent limb to that eye
cards.explanation: Because light in the right eye constricts both pupils, both motor limbs and both iris muscles must be working, so the problem has to be on the sensory side. Since light in the left eye produces nothing at all, the signal is never leaving that eye, which places the lesion in the left optic nerve. A left CN III lesion would leave the left pupil fixed even when the right eye is lit, which is not what happened. A right optic nerve lesion would abolish the response to right sided light, and a right CN III lesion would leave the right pupil fixed.

cards.q: In an older adult the lens has hardened and can no longer round up, although the ciliary muscle still contracts normally. When this person looks at a near object, what happens?
cards.a: Refractive power stays near its distance value and the near image falls behind the retina.
options: Refractive power stays near its distance value and the near image falls behind the retina
Refractive power rises normally and the near image falls on the retina
Refractive power drops below its distance value and the near image falls in front of the retina
Refractive power rises too far and the near image falls in front of the retina
cards.explanation: Ciliary contraction only slackens the zonules, so the shape change depends on the elasticity of the lens itself, and a stiff lens stays flat no matter how hard the muscle works. With power stuck at the distance setting, the strongly diverging rays from a near object are still converging when they pass the retina, so the focal point lands behind it and near print blurs. Power cannot fall below the resting value, because nothing pulls the lens flatter than the fully tensed zonules do. Excess power with a focal point in front of the retina describes myopia, which is the opposite problem.

cards.q: A drug that stimulates muscarinic receptors is placed in the eye. Trace its effect on the ciliary muscle, the lens, and the focus of the eye.
cards.a: The ciliary muscle contracts, the lens rounds, and the eye is locked in near focus.
options: The ciliary muscle relaxes, the lens flattens, and the eye is set for distance
The ciliary muscle contracts, the lens rounds, and the eye is locked in near focus
The ciliary muscle relaxes, the lens rounds, and the eye is set for near
The ciliary muscle contracts, the lens flattens, and the eye is set for distance
cards.explanation: A muscarinic agonist mimics the parasympathetic input, so the ciliary ring contracts, the zonules slacken, the elastic lens rounds up, and refractive power rises to its near setting and stays there. Distance objects then focus in front of the retina and look blurred, which patients describe as an induced nearsightedness. The two options that pair contraction with flattening or relaxation with rounding break the link between zonular tension and lens shape, and full relaxation with distance focus is what a muscarinic blocker would produce.

cards.q: Which molecule inside a rod actually absorbs the photon?
cards.a: Retinal.
options: Retinal
Opsin
Transducin
Guanylyl cyclase
cards.explanation: Retinal is the light absorbing chromophore, a derivative of vitamin A, and its shape change is the only step in vision that light itself performs. Opsin is the protein that holds retinal and shapes which wavelengths it absorbs best, but opsin alone does not capture the photon. Transducin is the G protein activated afterward, and guanylyl cyclase is the enzyme that rebuilds cyclic GMP during recovery.

cards.q: What two parts make up rhodopsin?
cards.a: The protein opsin plus 11-cis retinal.
options: The protein opsin plus all-trans retinal
The protein transducin plus cyclic GMP
The protein opsin plus 11-cis retinal
The enzyme phosphodiesterase plus 11-cis retinal
cards.explanation: Rhodopsin is a G protein coupled receptor, opsin, with 11-cis retinal bound in its core as a built in ligand waiting to be changed by light. All-trans retinal is the product formed after a photon is absorbed, and once it forms, the pigment is bleached rather than resting. Transducin and phosphodiesterase are downstream signaling proteins, not components of the pigment itself.

cards.q: What happens to retinal when it absorbs a photon?
cards.a: It isomerizes from the 11-cis form to the all-trans form.
options: It is phosphorylated and released from the disc membrane
It isomerizes from the all-trans form to the 11-cis form
It isomerizes from the 11-cis form to the all-trans form
It binds a molecule of cyclic GMP and changes charge
cards.explanation: The photon straightens a bend in the retinal molecule, converting 11-cis to all-trans, and that new shape forces a conformational change in the surrounding opsin that activates it. The reverse conversion, all-trans back to 11-cis, happens later in the pigment epithelium during regeneration and requires energy rather than light. Retinal is not phosphorylated by the photon, and it never binds cyclic GMP.

cards.q: Which G protein does activated rhodopsin turn on?
cards.a: Transducin.
options: Gustducin
Transducin
Golf
Calmodulin
cards.explanation: Transducin is the retina specific G protein, and activated rhodopsin loads it with GTP so that its alpha subunit can go on to switch on phosphodiesterase. Gustducin does the same kind of job in taste receptor cells for bitter, sweet, and umami. Golf serves olfactory receptor neurons. Calmodulin is a calcium binding protein, not a G protein at all.

cards.q: What does the phosphodiesterase activated during phototransduction do?
cards.a: It breaks down cyclic GMP.
options: It synthesizes cyclic GMP from GTP
It breaks down cyclic GMP
It phosphorylates the cation channel
It converts all-trans retinal back to 11-cis retinal
cards.explanation: Phosphodiesterase hydrolyzes cyclic GMP to 5 prime GMP, which drops the concentration of the messenger that was holding the cation channels open. Building cyclic GMP from GTP is the job of guanylyl cyclase, the opposing enzyme that restores the resting state. The channel is gated by cyclic GMP binding directly, not by phosphorylation, and regeneration of 11-cis retinal happens in the pigment epithelium through separate enzymes.

cards.q: When light strikes a photoreceptor, which way does the cyclic GMP concentration go?
cards.a: It falls.
options: It falls
It rises
It rises briefly and then returns to the dark level
It does not change, because cyclic AMP carries the signal instead
cards.explanation: Light activates phosphodiesterase, so cyclic GMP is destroyed faster than it is made and its concentration drops. That fall is the core of the whole cascade, because the cation channels only stay open while cyclic GMP is bound to them. A rise in cyclic GMP is what happens in the dark and during recovery after the light goes off. Cyclic AMP is the messenger in olfactory receptor neurons, not in photoreceptors.

cards.q: How does the membrane potential of a photoreceptor respond to light?
cards.a: It hyperpolarizes.
options: It depolarizes to threshold and fires an action potential
It stays constant while the firing rate rises
It depolarizes without firing an action potential
It hyperpolarizes
cards.explanation: Light closes the cyclic GMP gated cation channels, which removes a steady inward positive current, so the inside of the cell becomes more negative. This is the single most counterintuitive fact in the visual system, because every other sensory receptor you have studied depolarizes to its stimulus. Photoreceptors also do not fire action potentials at all, so any answer built on threshold or firing rate misdescribes how they signal.

cards.q: Which neurotransmitter do photoreceptors release onto bipolar cells?
cards.a: Glutamate.
options: GABA
Glutamate
Dopamine
Acetylcholine
cards.explanation: Photoreceptors release glutamate continuously in the dark and release less of it in the light, so the message the retina sends inward is written in changes to a steady glutamate stream. GABA and dopamine are used by amacrine and horizontal cells for lateral processing within the retina, not by photoreceptors. Acetylcholine appears at neuromuscular junctions and in autonomic ganglia rather than at the photoreceptor terminal.

cards.q: In complete darkness, what is happening at the cyclic GMP gated channels of a rod?
cards.a: Cyclic GMP is high, the channels are open, and Na+ and Ca2+ flow in.
options: Cyclic GMP is high, the channels are open, and Na+ and Ca2+ flow in
Cyclic GMP is low, the channels are closed, and no current flows
Cyclic GMP is high, the channels are open, and K+ flows out
Cyclic GMP is low, the channels are open, and Cl- flows in
cards.explanation: With no light there is nothing to activate phosphodiesterase, so cyclic GMP stays high, holds the channels open, and lets a steady inward flow of Na+ and Ca2+ called the dark current keep the cell near minus 40 mV. That is a depolarized resting state compared with most neurons. Low cyclic GMP with closed channels describes the illuminated cell instead. The channels are cation channels, so they do not carry outward K+ or inward Cl- as their main current.

cards.q: Cyclic GMP falls inside a cone. What happens to the cation channels in its outer segment?
cards.a: They close, because cyclic GMP must stay bound to hold them open.
options: They open wider, because cyclic GMP normally blocks them
They close, because cyclic GMP must stay bound to hold them open
They stay open, because the channels are voltage gated rather than ligand gated
They close, but only after the cell has fired an action potential
cards.explanation: These channels are ligand gated from the inside, and cyclic GMP is the ligand that props them open, so losing the ligand lets them shut. Treating cyclic GMP as a blocker reverses the logic and would predict depolarization to light. The channels are not voltage gated, which is why the response is graded with light intensity. Photoreceptors never fire action potentials, so nothing about channel closure waits on a spike.

cards.q: A steady light is turned on over a rod. What happens to the amount of glutamate released from its terminal?
cards.a: It decreases, because hyperpolarization reduces Ca2+ entry at the terminal.
options: It increases, because the cell is more strongly stimulated
It increases, because closing cation channels traps Ca2+ inside the terminal
It stays the same, because release is independent of membrane potential
It decreases, because hyperpolarization reduces Ca2+ entry at the terminal
cards.explanation: Release from the photoreceptor terminal depends on voltage gated Ca2+ channels, and hyperpolarization closes them, so less Ca2+ enters and fewer vesicles fuse. The intuitive answer, that a stimulated cell releases more transmitter, is exactly the trap this system sets, because in vision the stimulus reduces output. Release is strictly voltage dependent through Ca2+, and closing the outer segment channels lowers rather than raises internal Ca2+.

cards.q: A drug inhibits the phosphodiesterase in rod outer segments. What happens when light then strikes those rods?
cards.a: Cyclic GMP stays high, the channels stay open, and the light response fails.
options: Cyclic GMP falls faster, so the light response is exaggerated
Cyclic GMP stays high, the channels stay open, and the light response fails
Cyclic GMP stays high, so the rods hyperpolarize even in darkness
Cyclic GMP falls, but glutamate release rises instead of falling in the light
cards.explanation: Phosphodiesterase is the step that translates photon capture into a drop in cyclic GMP, so blocking it leaves the messenger high, the channels open, and the cell stuck in something close to its dark state no matter what the light does. Blocking an enzyme cannot speed up the reaction it catalyzes. High cyclic GMP holds cells depolarized rather than hyperpolarized. Glutamate release always tracks membrane potential, so it cannot rise while the cell hyperpolarizes.

cards.q: A patient's diet has been low in vitamin A for months. What is the expected effect on rod function?
cards.a: Less 11-cis retinal is available, so rhodopsin is scarce and dim light vision suffers.
options: Transducin is not made, so the cascade cannot be switched off
Less 11-cis retinal is available, so rhodopsin is scarce and dim light vision suffers
Cyclic GMP cannot be synthesized, so the rods stay hyperpolarized
The rods lose their cyclic GMP gated channels, so the dark current disappears entirely
cards.explanation: Retinal is made from vitamin A, so a shortage limits how much functional rhodopsin can be assembled, and rods with too little pigment capture too few photons in dim conditions. This is why night blindness is the earliest sign of vitamin A deficiency. Transducin, guanylyl cyclase, and the cation channels are all proteins whose synthesis does not depend on vitamin A, so none of them is the limiting step here.

cards.q: An ON bipolar cell carries metabotropic glutamate receptors that hyperpolarize it when glutamate binds. What does light do to that bipolar cell?
cards.a: It depolarizes it, because the photoreceptor releases less glutamate.
options: It hyperpolarizes it, because the photoreceptor hyperpolarizes too
It hyperpolarizes it, because glutamate release rises in the light
It has no effect, because bipolar cells respond only to direct light
It depolarizes it, because the photoreceptor releases less glutamate
cards.explanation: The photoreceptor hyperpolarizes and releases less glutamate, and because glutamate was inhibiting this bipolar cell, removing it lets the bipolar cell depolarize. Sign inversion at this synapse is how the retina turns a light off signal into a light on signal. Assuming the bipolar cell must follow the photoreceptor in the same direction ignores the receptor type on the postsynaptic side. Bipolar cells sit deeper in the retina and do not absorb light themselves, and glutamate release falls rather than rises in light.

cards.q: During light exposure, intracellular Ca2+ in a photoreceptor falls. How does that help the cell adapt?
cards.a: Low Ca2+ releases guanylyl cyclase from inhibition, so cyclic GMP is rebuilt.
options: Low Ca2+ releases guanylyl cyclase from inhibition, so cyclic GMP is rebuilt
Low Ca2+ activates phosphodiesterase further, deepening the response
Low Ca2+ triggers more glutamate release to warn the bipolar cell
Low Ca2+ converts all-trans retinal back to 11-cis inside the outer segment
cards.explanation: Ca2+ normally restrains guanylyl cyclase, so when the channels close and Ca2+ entry stops, the cyclase speeds up and pushes cyclic GMP back toward its dark level, which reopens channels and resets sensitivity during a steady light. This negative feedback is why you can still see detail in bright sunlight instead of saturating. Deepening the response would be positive feedback, glutamate release falls rather than rises, and retinal regeneration takes place in the pigment epithelium with its own enzymes.

cards.q: Which sequence correctly orders the steps of phototransduction after a photon is absorbed?
cards.a: Retinal isomerizes, transducin activates phosphodiesterase, cyclic GMP falls, channels close, the cell hyperpolarizes, glutamate release drops.
options: Retinal isomerizes, transducin activates phosphodiesterase, cyclic GMP falls, channels close, the cell hyperpolarizes, glutamate release drops
Retinal isomerizes, cyclic GMP rises, channels open, the cell depolarizes, glutamate release rises
Transducin isomerizes retinal, phosphodiesterase makes cyclic GMP, channels open, the cell hyperpolarizes, glutamate rises
Retinal isomerizes, phosphodiesterase is inhibited, cyclic GMP rises, the channels close, the cell hyperpolarizes, and glutamate release drops
cards.explanation: Each step follows from the one before it: the shape change activates opsin, opsin activates transducin, transducin frees phosphodiesterase, the messenger is destroyed, the channels that needed it shut, the loss of inward current hyperpolarizes the cell, and less depolarization means less Ca2+ and less glutamate. A sequence in which cyclic GMP rises and the cell depolarizes reverses every direction and describes the dark state instead. A sequence in which transducin isomerizes retinal scrambles which molecule acts on which. Any sequence pairing a rise in cyclic GMP with channel closure is impossible, which cannot happen because cyclic GMP is what holds those channels open.

cards.q: A mutation leaves the cyclic GMP gated cation channels of a rod permanently open regardless of cyclic GMP. Predict the rod's behavior in light.
cards.a: It stays depolarized and keeps releasing glutamate, so light produces no signal.
options: It hyperpolarizes more strongly than normal, so light signals are exaggerated
It stays depolarized and keeps releasing glutamate, so light produces no signal
It hyperpolarizes normally, because glutamate release does not depend on the channels
It depolarizes further in light, so the bipolar cell receives a reversed signal
cards.explanation: The only way light changes the membrane potential is by closing those channels, so a channel that ignores cyclic GMP leaves the dark current running and the cell locked near minus 40 mV with tonic glutamate output. The upstream cascade still runs, but its output has nowhere to act. Exaggerated hyperpolarization would require more channel closure, not less. Glutamate release depends on membrane potential through Ca2+ channels, so it cannot change while the potential is fixed, and nothing in this mutation drives the cell further positive during light.

cards.q: A toxin locks transducin in its active state in a group of cones. Predict cyclic GMP, the channels, the membrane potential, and glutamate release in complete darkness.
cards.a: Cyclic GMP low, channels closed, cell hyperpolarized, glutamate release reduced.
options: Cyclic GMP high, channels open, cell depolarized, glutamate release high
Cyclic GMP low, channels closed, cell depolarized, glutamate release high
Cyclic GMP low, channels closed, cell hyperpolarized, glutamate release reduced
Cyclic GMP high, channels closed, cell hyperpolarized, glutamate release reduced
cards.explanation: Active transducin keeps phosphodiesterase running, so cyclic GMP is destroyed even with no photons, and the cell behaves as though a bright light were shining on it: channels shut, membrane hyperpolarized, transmitter output down. High cyclic GMP with open channels and heavy glutamate release is the true dark state, which this cell can no longer reach. Pairing closed channels with depolarization contradicts the loss of inward current. Pairing high cyclic GMP with closed channels is impossible, because cyclic GMP is the ligand holding those channels open.

cards.q: A student objects that hyperpolarizing to light means the rod is sending less information when the stimulus arrives. What is the best answer?
cards.a: The rod releases glutamate tonically in darkness, so the retina reads the drop in release as the light signal.
options: The rod switches to action potentials in bright light, which carry the information instead
The rod releases glutamate tonically in darkness, so the retina reads the drop in release as the light signal
The rod releases a second transmitter during hyperpolarization, so the message still gets through to the bipolar cell
Hyperpolarization is too small to matter, and the real signal comes from the pigment epithelium
cards.explanation: Information sits in the change, not in the absolute direction, and because the rod is depolarized and releasing glutamate steadily in the dark, any reduction in that stream is a clear message to bipolar cells. Sign inverting ON bipolar cells then turn the decrease into a depolarization, so the pathway reaches the ganglion cells as an increase in firing. Photoreceptors never fire action potentials and release only glutamate, and the pigment epithelium supports the photoreceptors metabolically rather than signaling to the retina.

cards.q: Which photoreceptor type operates in dim light?
cards.a: Rods.
options: Cones
Bipolar cells
Rods
Ganglion cells
cards.explanation: Rods carry far more pigment per cell and pool their signals, so they respond to very few photons and are the only photoreceptors working under starlight. Cones need much brighter light and go silent in dim conditions, which is why color drains out of a dark room. Bipolar and ganglion cells are second and third order neurons in the retina and do not absorb light at all.

cards.q: Which photoreceptor type provides color vision?
cards.a: Cones, which come in three types with different pigments.
options: Cones, which come in three types with different pigments
Rods, which come in three types with different pigments
Rods, which change pigment with wavelength
Cones, which all share one pigment and code color by firing rate
cards.explanation: Color comes from comparing the outputs of three cone classes whose photopsins peak at short, medium, and long wavelengths, so the brain reads a ratio rather than a single value. Rods all carry the same pigment, rhodopsin, which is why rod vision is monochrome no matter what wavelength arrives. A single pigment cannot signal wavelength through firing rate either, because a dim light of the best wavelength and a bright light of a poor one give the same response.

cards.q: Which region of the retina gives the sharpest vision?
cards.a: The fovea centralis.
options: The optic disc
The peripheral retina
The fovea centralis
The ora serrata
cards.explanation: The fovea is packed with cones, has almost no convergence onto bipolar cells, and the overlying retinal layers are pushed aside, so it resolves the finest detail. The optic disc is where the axons leave and has no photoreceptors at all, making it the blind spot. The peripheral retina is rod dominated and pools heavily, which trades acuity for sensitivity, and the ora serrata is simply the front edge of the retina.

cards.q: Whose axons form the optic nerve?
cards.a: Retinal ganglion cells.
options: Photoreceptors
Retinal ganglion cells
Amacrine cells
Bipolar cells
cards.explanation: Ganglion cells are the only retinal neurons that fire action potentials and send axons out of the eye, and those axons converge at the optic disc to become the optic nerve. Photoreceptors and bipolar cells signal with graded potentials over very short distances inside the retina. Amacrine cells modify signals laterally at the bipolar to ganglion cell layer and stay within the retina.

cards.q: Which fibers cross to the other side at the optic chiasm?
cards.a: Fibers from the nasal half of each retina.
options: Fibers from the temporal half of each retina
Fibers from the nasal half of each retina
All fibers from the left eye only
Every fiber from both eyes
cards.explanation: Nasal retinal fibers, which carry the temporal visual field of each eye, cross at the chiasm, while temporal retinal fibers stay on their own side. That partial crossing is what puts the entire left visual field of both eyes into the right optic tract. If every fiber crossed, each hemisphere would receive one whole eye rather than one half of the world, and a lesion anywhere behind the chiasm would blind one eye instead of one field.

cards.q: Which thalamic nucleus relays visual information to the cortex?
cards.a: The lateral geniculate nucleus.
options: The lateral geniculate nucleus
The ventral posterolateral nucleus
The medial geniculate nucleus
The ventral posteromedial nucleus
cards.explanation: Optic tract fibers synapse in the lateral geniculate nucleus, and its neurons project through the optic radiations to the occipital cortex. The medial geniculate nucleus is the matching relay for hearing. The ventral posterolateral nucleus handles body somatosensation and the ventral posteromedial nucleus handles the face and taste, so neither carries vision.

cards.q: Where is the primary visual cortex located?
cards.a: In the occipital lobe.
options: In the temporal lobe
In the frontal lobe
In the parietal lobe
In the occipital lobe
cards.explanation: The optic radiations end in the cortex around the calcarine sulcus of the occipital lobe, at the back of the brain. The temporal lobe holds primary auditory cortex, and parts of it handle later object recognition rather than the first cortical step. The parietal lobe holds somatosensory cortex, and the frontal lobe holds motor areas.

cards.q: What causes the blind spot in each eye?
cards.a: The optic disc contains no photoreceptors.
options: The optic disc contains no photoreceptors
The fovea contains no rods
The lens casts a shadow on the central retina
Blood vessels block light over the macula
cards.explanation: At the optic disc the ganglion cell axons gather and exit the eye, so there is no room for rods or cones, and any image landing there is not detected. The fovea does lack rods, which affects dim light vision at the center of gaze but leaves plenty of cones, so it is not blind. The lens is transparent and casts no shadow, and although retinal vessels do run in front of the photoreceptors, they are too fine and too stable to create a discrete blind area.

cards.q: Why is rod vision less sharp than cone vision?
cards.a: Many rods converge onto one bipolar cell, so fine detail is pooled away.
options: Rods are spread evenly across the retina instead of clustering near the center
Rods respond more slowly to a change in light intensity
Many rods converge onto one bipolar cell, so fine detail is pooled away
Rods lack the pigment needed to absorb photons efficiently
cards.explanation: Convergence sums the output of a wide patch of retina onto a single output neuron, which raises sensitivity but destroys information about which rod in the patch was hit. Foveal cones approach a one to one line to the brain, which preserves position. Rods are actually more sensitive and carry more pigment than cones, so the explanation cannot be a shortage of pigment, and their slower response affects motion blur rather than spatial resolution.

cards.q: On a clear night a faint star disappears when you look straight at it and reappears when you look slightly to one side. Why?
cards.a: The fovea has no rods, so a very dim point is detected only by peripheral retina.
options: Cones adapt within a second or two and stop responding to a steady point of light
The blind spot sits at the center of gaze and swallows the image
The lens cannot focus a point source onto the fovea
The fovea has no rods, so a very dim point is detected only by peripheral retina
cards.explanation: Looking straight at something places its image on the fovea, which is all cones, and cones are too insensitive for starlight, so the star vanishes. Shifting your gaze a few degrees moves the image onto rod rich retina, where convergence pools enough photons to register. The blind spot lies about 15 degrees to the nasal side of the fovea, not at the center of gaze, and normal optics focus a distant point perfectly well on the fovea.

cards.q: A lesion completely destroys the left optic nerve. What visual deficit results?
cards.a: Total blindness of the left eye.
options: Loss of the left half of the field in both eyes
Loss of the temporal field of both eyes
Total blindness of the left eye
Loss of the right half of the field in both eyes
cards.explanation: In front of the chiasm every fiber in the nerve comes from one eye, so cutting it removes all input from that eye and nothing from the other, and the patient is blind in the left eye alone. Losing one half of the field in both eyes requires a lesion behind the chiasm, where fibers from the two eyes have already been sorted by field rather than by eye. Loss of both temporal fields is the signature of a lesion at the chiasm itself.

cards.q: A pituitary tumor grows upward and compresses the center of the optic chiasm. What field deficit results?
cards.a: Bitemporal hemianopia, loss of the temporal field of each eye.
options: Left homonymous hemianopia, loss of the left field of both eyes
Right homonymous hemianopia, loss of the right field of both eyes
Blindness of the right eye, with the left eye unaffected
Bitemporal hemianopia, loss of the temporal field of each eye
cards.explanation: The crossing fibers in the middle of the chiasm come from the nasal half of each retina, and the nasal retina views the temporal side of the world, so compressing them cuts out the outer field of both eyes. Patients describe it as tunnel like side vision, sometimes noticed first by bumping into door frames. A homonymous hemianopia requires a lesion of a tract or radiation behind the chiasm, and blindness of a single eye requires a lesion of that eye's optic nerve.

cards.q: The right optic tract is severed just behind the chiasm. What field deficit results?
cards.a: Left homonymous hemianopia, loss of the left half of the field in both eyes.
options: Right homonymous hemianopia, loss of the right half of the field in both eyes
Bitemporal hemianopia
Blindness of the right eye
Left homonymous hemianopia, loss of the left half of the field in both eyes
cards.explanation: The right optic tract carries fibers from the right half of each retina, and the right retina looks at the left half of the world, so the deficit is contralateral and the same half of the field is lost in both eyes. Naming the right field reverses the retina to world relationship, which is the most common error on this competency. Bitemporal loss is the chiasm pattern, and monocular blindness is the optic nerve pattern.

cards.q: A disease selectively destroys cones in the fovea while sparing rods. What is the expected pattern of vision loss?
cards.a: Loss of central detail and color vision, with dim peripheral vision preserved.
options: Loss of central detail and color vision, with dim peripheral vision preserved
Loss of peripheral vision at night, with sharp central vision preserved
Total blindness, because all visual input passes through the fovea
Loss of the temporal half of the field in the affected eye
cards.explanation: Foveal cones supply reading acuity and color, so losing them takes out the center of the visual world and leaves a functional but coarse rod driven surround. Patients often keep enough peripheral vision to walk around while being unable to read a page. Losing night and peripheral vision while keeping central acuity is the opposite pattern and points to rod loss. Nothing about photoreceptor loss respects a vertical field boundary, so a hemianopia is not expected.

cards.q: A patient has lost the left half of the visual field in both eyes, with normal pupillary light reflexes. Where is the lesion?
cards.a: In the right optic tract.
options: In the left optic nerve
In the optic chiasm
In the right optic tract
In the left optic tract
cards.explanation: A deficit in the same half of the field in both eyes must be behind the chiasm, because only there are fibers grouped by field rather than by eye, and losing the left field means losing the pathway on the right. The left optic tract would remove the right half of both fields instead. A chiasm lesion would produce bitemporal loss, and a left optic nerve lesion would blind that eye alone rather than half of each field.

cards.q: Trace why a tumor at the optic chiasm produces loss of both temporal fields. Which fibers are damaged and what did they view?
cards.a: The crossing nasal retinal fibers, which viewed the temporal half of each visual field.
options: The uncrossed temporal retinal fibers, which viewed the nasal half of each field
All fibers of the right optic nerve, which viewed the entire right field
The crossing nasal retinal fibers, which viewed the temporal half of each visual field
The crossing temporal retinal fibers, which viewed the temporal half of each field
cards.explanation: Light from the temporal side of the world crosses the pupil and lands on the nasal retina, and those nasal fibers are exactly the ones that decussate in the middle of the chiasm, so central compression takes out both temporal fields. Temporal retinal fibers run along the outer edges of the chiasm and stay uncrossed, so they survive a central lesion. Calling the crossing fibers temporal confuses the retinal name with the field name, which is the trap in this whole topic.

cards.q: You walk from bright sunlight into a dark theater. Vision is poor at first and improves over the next 20 to 30 minutes. What accounts for the slow phase of this adaptation?
cards.a: Rhodopsin is regenerated in rods, which slowly restores their high sensitivity.
options: The pupil dilates fully, which takes about half an hour
New rod cells are produced to replace the ones that were bleached by bright sunlight
Cones gradually take over from rods as the eye cools
Rhodopsin is regenerated in rods, which slowly restores their high sensitivity
cards.explanation: Bright light bleaches rhodopsin faster than it can be rebuilt, so on entering the dark the rods are nearly pigment free and must regenerate 11-cis retinal, a chemical process that takes tens of minutes. Cone adaptation is largely finished within a few minutes, which is why you can see something almost immediately but not the dim details. Pupillary dilation is complete in seconds, and photoreceptors are not replaced on this timescale.

cards.q: A patient reads the smallest line of an eye chart in a bright room but bumps into furniture in dim hallways. Testing shows rod function is nearly absent while cones are normal. Predict daytime acuity, night peripheral vision, and color vision.
cards.a: Daytime acuity normal, night peripheral vision poor, color vision normal.
options: Daytime acuity poor, night peripheral vision normal, color vision poor
Daytime acuity poor, night peripheral vision poor, color vision normal
Daytime acuity normal, night peripheral vision normal, color vision poor
Daytime acuity normal, night peripheral vision poor, color vision normal
cards.explanation: Cones supply high acuity and color under bright light, so both stay intact when only rods are lost. Rods supply the sensitive, rod dominated periphery, so dim conditions and side vision are where the deficit shows up. Predicting poor color or poor daytime acuity would require cone loss, and predicting preserved night vision ignores that cones cannot respond at low light levels.

cards.q: In myopia, where do parallel rays from a distant object come to a focus?
cards.a: In front of the retina.
options: In front of the retina
Exactly on the retina
Behind the retina
On the optic disc
cards.explanation: A myopic eye has too much refractive power for its length, usually because the eyeball is too long or the cornea too steep, so distant rays converge early and are already spreading again by the time they reach the retina. Focus behind the retina is the hyperopic pattern. Focus exactly on the retina defines the normal eye, and the optic disc is a location on the retina rather than a focal plane.

cards.q: In hyperopia, where do parallel rays from a distant object come to a focus?
cards.a: Behind the retina.
options: In front of the retina
Behind the retina
On the lens surface
Exactly on the retina
cards.explanation: A hyperopic eye is optically too weak for its length, usually because the eyeball is short, so the rays are still converging when they pass the photoreceptor layer and the theoretical focal point lies behind it. Focus in front of the retina is myopia, the opposite error. Light never focuses on the lens surface, since the lens is part of the focusing system rather than a screen.

cards.q: Which type of corrective lens is used for myopia?
cards.a: A concave, diverging lens.
options: A convex, converging lens
A cylindrical lens
A prism
A concave, diverging lens
cards.explanation: The myopic eye has too much power, so the correction must subtract power by spreading the rays slightly before they enter the eye, which pushes the focal point back onto the retina. A convex lens adds power and would make myopia worse, although it is exactly what hyperopia needs. Cylindrical lenses correct unequal curvature in astigmatism, and prisms shift image position for alignment problems rather than fixing focus.

cards.q: Which type of corrective lens is used for hyperopia?
cards.a: A convex, converging lens.
options: A concave, diverging lens
A flat lens with a tinted coating
A cylindrical lens
A convex, converging lens
cards.explanation: The hyperopic eye needs more refractive power, so a converging lens starts the rays inward before they reach the cornea and brings the focal point forward onto the retina. A concave lens removes power and would drive the focus even farther back. Cylindrical lenses address astigmatism, and a tint changes light intensity without changing where the image forms.

cards.q: What is the underlying cause of presbyopia?
cards.a: The lens loses elasticity with age and can no longer round up.
options: The lens loses elasticity with age and can no longer round up
The eyeball elongates with age
The cornea becomes irregular in curvature with age
The pupil dilates more widely with age
cards.explanation: Lens proteins accumulate and cross link over decades, so the lens stiffens and stops springing into a rounder shape when the zonules slacken, which is why the near point recedes after roughly age 40. The ciliary muscle still contracts, so the failure is in the lens rather than the motor supply. Elongation of the eyeball is myopia, irregular corneal curvature is astigmatism, and the aging pupil in fact becomes smaller rather than larger.

cards.q: What is the usual cause of astigmatism?
cards.a: The cornea is more curved in one meridian than another.
options: The eyeball is too long from front to back
The lens has hardened and cannot change shape
The cornea is more curved in one meridian than another
The retina is detached at its outer edge
cards.explanation: A normal cornea is close to spherical, and when one meridian is steeper than the one at right angles to it, light in the two planes focuses at different distances, so no single plane is sharp. That is why patients see lines in one orientation more clearly than lines in another. Excess axial length is myopia, a hardened lens is presbyopia, and retinal detachment causes field loss rather than a refractive error.

cards.q: Which type of lens corrects astigmatism?
cards.a: A cylindrical lens.
options: A cylindrical lens
A spherical convex lens
A spherical concave lens
A bifocal lens
cards.explanation: A cylindrical lens has power in only one meridian, so it can add or subtract power along the axis that is out of step and leave the other axis alone. Spherical lenses change power equally in every meridian, so they can move both focal planes but cannot bring them together. A bifocal simply puts two spherical powers in one frame, usually for presbyopia.

cards.q: What does emmetropia describe?
cards.a: An eye that focuses distant objects on the retina with the lens relaxed.
options: An eye whose near point has receded past 40 cm
An eye that must accommodate constantly to see distant objects
An eye with equal curvature in every corneal meridian but a short axis
An eye that focuses distant objects on the retina with the lens relaxed
cards.explanation: Emmetropia is the normal state, where axial length and refractive power match, so no effort and no correction are needed for distance vision. An eye that must accommodate to see far away is hyperopic and is compensating rather than normal. A short axis is hyperopia even if the cornea is perfectly regular, and a receded near point is presbyopia.

cards.q: A patient's eyeball is longer than average from cornea to retina, and the cornea and lens are normal. Which condition is this and which vision is blurred?
cards.a: Myopia, with distance vision blurred.
options: Hyperopia, with distance vision blurred
Myopia, with distance vision blurred
Myopia, with near vision blurred
Hyperopia, with near vision blurred
cards.explanation: A long eye puts the retina behind the focal point of parallel rays, so distant objects blur while near objects, whose rays arrive diverging and focus farther back, can still land correctly. That is why nearsighted people can often read without glasses. Hyperopia comes from an eye that is too short, and blurred near vision with clear distance vision is the hyperopic or presbyopic pattern.

cards.q: A 50-year-old with previously excellent vision now holds the newspaper at arm's length to read it. What has happened and what correction helps?
cards.a: Presbyopia, corrected with a convex reading lens.
options: Myopia, corrected with a concave lens
Astigmatism, corrected with a cylindrical lens
Presbyopia, corrected with a convex reading lens
Hyperopia from a shortened eyeball, corrected with a prism
cards.explanation: Holding print farther away is the classic sign that the near point has receded, which happens as the aging lens stiffens and can no longer add power for close work. A convex lens supplies the extra convergence the lens can no longer produce. Myopia would blur distance rather than near vision, astigmatism blurs one orientation at every distance, and the eyeball does not shorten in adulthood.

cards.q: A concave spectacle lens is placed in front of a myopic eye. What does it do to the incoming rays and to the focal point?
cards.a: It diverges the rays slightly, moving the focal point back onto the retina.
options: It converges the rays, moving the focal point forward onto the retina
It diverges the rays slightly, moving the focal point back onto the retina
It converges the rays, increasing total refractive power
It bends rays in only one meridian, evening out the two focal planes
cards.explanation: The myopic eye already focuses too early, so the correction must reduce net power, and diverging the rays before they hit the cornea delays convergence until the retinal plane. Converging the rays would add power and worsen the error. Bending light in only one meridian describes a cylindrical lens, which is the fix for astigmatism rather than for excess spherical power.

cards.q: A patient's cornea is steeper along the vertical meridian than the horizontal one. What visual complaint does this predict?
cards.a: Lines in one orientation look sharp while lines at right angles look blurred.
options: Lines in one orientation look sharp while lines at right angles look blurred
Distance vision is uniformly blurred while near vision remains sharp and clear
Vision is sharp in bright light and blurred in dim light
Central vision is lost while peripheral vision remains
cards.explanation: With two different curvatures the eye has two focal planes, so whichever plane lands on the retina gives a sharp image while the other stays out of focus, and the effect follows the orientation of the detail being viewed. Uniform blur at distance with sharp near vision is myopia, where power is excessive in every meridian equally. Light dependent blur points to pupil size and photoreceptor issues, and central field loss is a retinal problem rather than a refractive one.

cards.q: A young adult with mild hyperopia sees clearly at distance but reports headaches and eye fatigue after reading. Why?
cards.a: Accommodation is needed even for distance, so near work demands sustained extra effort.
options: The lens is already fully rounded at rest, so no reserve remains
Accommodation is needed even for distance, so near work demands sustained extra effort
The pupil cannot constrict during near work, so glare from the page tires the eyes quickly
The eyeball lengthens during reading and then rebounds
cards.explanation: A hyperopic eye is underpowered, so the ciliary muscle must contract just to bring distant objects onto the retina, and reading requires piling more accommodation on top of that, which the muscle cannot sustain comfortably. Young patients can do it, which is why the acuity looks normal, but the effort shows up as strain. The lens at rest is flat, not fully rounded, the pupil constricts normally in these patients, and the eyeball does not change length during reading.

cards.q: A myopic student takes off her glasses and finds she can still read a book held 20 cm from her face without any blur. Explain.
cards.a: Her excess refractive power suits the diverging rays from a near object.
options: Her ciliary muscle relaxes fully, which adds power for near work
Removing the glasses lets the pupil dilate, which sharpens the retinal image
Her excess refractive power suits the diverging rays from a near object
Her eyeball shortens when she looks at something close
cards.explanation: Myopia means too much power for parallel rays, but rays from a close object are diverging when they arrive, and they need exactly that extra power, so at some near distance the image lands on the retina with no correction at all. This is why myopia is called nearsightedness. A relaxed ciliary muscle reduces lens power rather than adding it, pupil dilation reduces depth of focus, and the eyeball length is fixed.

cards.q: A healthy 20-year-old sees distant objects clearly but says print blurs unless it is held far away. Testing shows the ciliary muscle and lens elasticity are normal for age. What is the most likely explanation?
cards.a: Hyperopia, where the eye is optically too weak and accommodation is used up on distance.
options: Presbyopia, because the lens has already stiffened
Myopia, because the eyeball is longer than normal
Hyperopia, where the eye is optically too weak and accommodation is used up on distance
Astigmatism, because two corneal meridians bring light to a focus at different distances
cards.explanation: Blurred near vision with clear distance vision in someone whose lens is still elastic points to an underpowered eye rather than a failing accommodative mechanism, and hyperopia does exactly that by consuming accommodative reserve on far targets. Presbyopia produces the same symptom but requires a stiffened lens, which the testing has ruled out at this age. Myopia would blur distance first, and astigmatism blurs particular orientations at all distances rather than sparing distance vision entirely.

cards.q: A refractive surgeon removes too much corneal tissue while treating a myopic patient. What is the expected new refractive state and its correction?
cards.a: Hyperopia, corrected with a convex lens.
options: Myopia that is worse than before, corrected with a stronger concave lens
Emmetropia, needing no correction
Astigmatism, corrected with a cylindrical lens
Hyperopia, corrected with a convex lens
cards.explanation: Flattening the cornea subtracts refractive power, so removing more tissue than needed pushes the focal point past the retina and turns an overpowered eye into an underpowered one. The fix is then a converging lens, the same correction a naturally short eye needs. More myopia would require added power rather than less. Astigmatism would follow only if the tissue removal were uneven between meridians, and hitting the retina exactly is the intended outcome that did not happen here.

cards.q: A patient reports blurred vision at every distance. A spherical lens sharpens vertical letter strokes but leaves horizontal strokes soft no matter what power is tried. What is going on?
cards.a: Astigmatism, because the two meridians focus at different distances.
options: Myopia, because a stronger concave lens has not yet been tried
Astigmatism, because the two meridians focus at different distances
Presbyopia, because accommodation fails only at near
Optic nerve damage, because the retina is receiving a degraded signal
cards.explanation: The telling detail is that changing spherical power trades one orientation for the other instead of sharpening both, which means the eye holds two focal planes at once and needs power added in only one meridian. Any purely spherical error, myopic or presbyopic, sharpens all orientations together once the right power is found. Optic nerve damage would not improve with any lens, since the image on the retina is already fine.

cards.q: A 60-year-old with lifelong myopia now finds she needs one prescription for driving and a different one for reading. Explain why a single lens no longer works.
cards.a: Presbyopia has removed her accommodative range, so near objects blur.
options: Her myopia has reversed, so she now needs a converging lens for distance work
Her cornea has become irregular, so each distance needs its own cylinder
Presbyopia has removed her accommodative range, so near objects blur
Her pupil no longer constricts, so depth of focus has collapsed at near
cards.explanation: A younger myope wearing full distance correction can still accommodate for near, so one lens covers both, but once the lens stiffens that reserve is gone and the distance correction becomes too weak for reading. The result is two prescriptions or a bifocal that adds plus power for near. Myopia does not reverse with age, an irregular cornea would blur both distances rather than separating them, and pupil changes alter depth of focus only slightly and would not create two separate prescriptions.

cards.q: In what order does vibration pass through the auditory ossicles?
cards.a: Malleus, then incus, then stapes.
options: Stapes, then incus, then malleus
Malleus, then incus, then stapes
Incus, then malleus, then stapes
Malleus, then stapes, then incus
cards.explanation: The malleus is attached to the tympanic membrane and receives the vibration first, passes it to the incus, and the incus drives the stapes against the oval window. Reversing the order would send energy from the inner ear outward, which is not how airborne sound is collected. Any order that puts the stapes before the incus breaks the physical chain, since the stapes is the only ossicle that contacts the cochlea.

cards.q: Which ossicle presses against the oval window?
cards.a: The stapes.
options: The malleus
The incus
The stapes
The tympanic membrane
cards.explanation: The footplate of the stapes sits in the oval window and pushes on the perilymph of the scala vestibuli, converting airborne vibration into a fluid pressure wave. The malleus is at the other end of the chain, on the eardrum, and the incus bridges the two. The tympanic membrane is not an ossicle at all but the membrane that starts the chain moving.

cards.q: Against which structure do the stereocilia of cochlear hair cells bend?
cards.a: The tectorial membrane.
options: The basilar membrane
The oval window membrane
The round window membrane
The tectorial membrane
cards.explanation: Hair cells sit on the basilar membrane with their stereocilia projecting up into the overlying tectorial membrane, so when the basilar membrane moves the two shear against each other and the stereocilia are deflected. The basilar membrane carries the cells rather than bending them. The oval and round windows are the entry and pressure relief points for the fluid and are nowhere near the stereocilia.

cards.q: Which ion enters cochlear hair cells through the mechanically gated channels at the tips of the stereocilia?
options: Na+
Ca2+
Cl-
K+
cards.explanation: Endolymph bathing the stereocilia is unusually rich in K+, so when the tip link channels open, K+ flows down its gradient into the cell and depolarizes it. This is the one place in the body where K+ entry, rather than exit, is the depolarizing step. Na+ would be the answer for most other receptor cells, Ca2+ enters later at the base to trigger transmitter release, and Cl- is not the gating ion here.

cards.q: Which cranial nerve carries auditory information from the cochlea to the brainstem?
cards.a: The vestibulocochlear nerve, CN VIII.
options: The facial nerve, CN VII
The glossopharyngeal nerve, CN IX
The trigeminal nerve, CN V
The vestibulocochlear nerve, CN VIII
cards.explanation: The cochlear branch of CN VIII carries the spiral ganglion axons that synapse on the hair cells. CN VII runs alongside it through the temporal bone and moves the facial muscles, including the stapedius, but it does not carry hearing. CN V supplies facial sensation and the tensor tympani, and CN IX carries taste and sensation from the posterior tongue and pharynx.

cards.q: What is coded by the position along the basilar membrane where vibration peaks?
cards.a: The pitch, or frequency, of the sound.
options: The pitch, or frequency, of the sound
The loudness of the sound
The direction the sound came from
The duration of the sound
cards.explanation: The basilar membrane varies in width and stiffness along its length, so each frequency sets up a traveling wave that peaks at a particular place, and the brain reads that place as pitch. Loudness is carried by how large the displacement is and how fast the afferents fire, not by where the peak sits. Direction is computed centrally by comparing the two ears, and duration is simply how long the response lasts.

cards.q: Which part of the basilar membrane responds best to high frequency sounds?
cards.a: The base, near the oval window.
options: The base, near the oval window
The apex, at the far tip of the cochlear spiral
The middle turn, halfway along the spiral
Every part equally, since frequency is coded by firing rate
cards.explanation: At the base the membrane is narrow and stiff, which suits rapid vibration, so high frequencies peak there and never travel far into the cochlea. The apex is wide and floppy and resonates with low frequencies. A uniform response would make a place code impossible, and firing rate alone cannot carry pitch because axons cannot fire fast enough to track high frequencies.

cards.q: Which cells are the main sensory receptors for hearing?
cards.a: The inner hair cells of the organ of Corti.
options: The outer hair cells of the organ of Corti
The supporting cells of the organ of Corti
The inner hair cells of the organ of Corti
The cells of the stria vascularis
cards.explanation: A single row of inner hair cells makes the great majority of synapses onto afferent fibers of the cochlear nerve, so they are the cells that report sound to the brain. The three rows of outer hair cells act mostly as an amplifier, changing length to sharpen the traveling wave rather than reporting it. Supporting cells hold the structure together, and the stria vascularis secretes endolymph and maintains its high K+.

cards.q: Why is the ossicular chain necessary rather than letting sound strike the oval window directly?
cards.a: It concentrates force from a large membrane onto a small window to move the fluid.
options: It concentrates force from a large membrane onto a small window to move the fluid
It slows the vibration so hair cells have time to respond
It converts sound waves into electrical signals before they reach the cochlear fluid
It filters out high frequencies that would damage the hair cells
cards.explanation: Fluid is much harder to move than air, so most airborne energy would simply reflect off the oval window, and the ossicles solve this by funneling the force collected over the wide tympanic membrane onto the much smaller stapes footplate, with the lever action of the bones adding a little more. The result is a pressure gain of roughly twenty fold. The ossicles do not slow, transduce, or filter the signal, since transduction happens at the hair cells.

cards.q: When the stapes pushes inward at the oval window, what must the round window do?
cards.a: Bulge outward, because cochlear fluid cannot be compressed.
options: Open a channel that lets perilymph drain into the middle ear
Push inward at the same time, to double the pressure wave
Stay rigid, so that pressure builds inside the cochlea
Bulge outward, because cochlear fluid cannot be compressed
cards.explanation: Perilymph is essentially incompressible in a bony tube, so unless something yields, the stapes cannot move and no traveling wave forms, and the flexible round window membrane is that release point. This is why scarring of the round window impairs hearing. Both windows moving inward together, or a rigid round window, would lock the fluid in place, and the window is a membrane rather than a drainage route.

cards.q: A pure low frequency tone is played. Where along the cochlea will the basilar membrane displacement be greatest?
cards.a: Near the apex, where the membrane is wide and floppy.
options: Near the base, where the membrane is narrow and stiff
Near the apex, where the membrane is wide and floppy
Uniformly along the entire length of the membrane
At the round window, where the wave is reflected
cards.explanation: Low frequencies travel farthest before their traveling wave peaks, because the apex has the mechanical properties that resonate slowly. The stiff base is tuned to high frequencies and passes low ones along without peaking. A uniform response would erase the place code, and the round window is a pressure release membrane rather than a tuned resonator.

cards.q: The same tone is played louder. What changes in the cochlea and in the auditory nerve?
cards.a: The basilar membrane moves further, hair cells depolarize more, and afferents fire faster.
options: The peak of the traveling wave shifts toward the base and firing stays constant
Hair cells hyperpolarize more deeply, which the brain reads as loudness
The basilar membrane moves further, hair cells depolarize more, and afferents fire faster
The stapes vibrates at a higher frequency and more hair cells hyperpolarize
cards.explanation: Loudness is amplitude, so a louder tone deflects the basilar membrane further at the same place, opens more transduction channels, produces a bigger receptor potential, and drives a higher firing rate in the afferent while also recruiting neighboring hair cells. The place of the peak marks pitch, so it does not move when only intensity changes. Hair cells signal sound by depolarizing when bent toward the tallest stereocilia, and frequency does not change with volume.

cards.q: Stereocilia are deflected away from the tallest one. What happens to the hair cell?
cards.a: Transduction channels close and the cell hyperpolarizes below its resting level.
options: Transduction channels close and the cell hyperpolarizes below its resting level
Transduction channels open more widely and the cell depolarizes
Nothing changes, because only bending toward the tallest one is detected
The cell fires an action potential in the opposite direction
cards.explanation: A fraction of the tip link channels are open at rest, so bending in one direction pulls them further open and bending the other way lets them shut, which drops K+ entry and hyperpolarizes the cell below baseline. That two way swing is how a hair cell follows the back and forth of a sound wave with graded changes in transmitter release. Nothing here opens channels, deflection in both directions is detected, and hair cells do not fire action potentials.

cards.q: Years of loud noise exposure destroy hair cells near the base of the cochlea. What hearing loss is expected?
cards.a: Loss of high frequency hearing, with low frequencies relatively spared.
options: Loss of high frequency hearing, with low frequencies relatively spared
Loss of low frequency hearing, with high frequencies relatively spared
Equal loss across all frequencies
Loss of the ability to judge loudness, with pitch intact
cards.explanation: The base of the cochlea is tuned to high frequencies, so damage there takes those frequencies out first while the apex, which handles low tones, keeps working. This is why noise damage and age related loss both show up first as trouble with consonants and high voices. Low frequency loss would require apical damage, and losing loudness perception while keeping pitch would require a coding failure rather than a loss of a tuned region.

cards.q: Endolymph has an unusually high K+ concentration. Why does that make K+ entry depolarizing in hair cells?
cards.a: The K+ gradient favors inward movement into the cell, carrying positive charge in.
options: High external K+ makes the channels close instead of open
K+ carries negative charge, so its entry lowers the internal charge
The K+ gradient favors inward movement into the cell, carrying positive charge in
K+ entry drags Cl- into the cell along with it, and Cl- is the actual depolarizing ion
cards.explanation: In most cells the outside is K+ poor, so open K+ channels let K+ leave and the cell hyperpolarizes, but the stria vascularis pumps K+ into endolymph until the gradient reverses at the tips of the stereocilia, so opening a channel there brings K+ in. Positive charge entering makes the interior less negative, which is depolarization. K+ is a cation, mechanically gated channels respond to tension rather than to external K+ concentration, and Cl- is not involved.

cards.q: Which sequence correctly traces a sound from the eardrum to the auditory nerve?
cards.a: Tympanic membrane, ossicles, oval window, perilymph wave, basilar membrane, stereocilia bending, hair cell depolarization, cochlear nerve firing.
options: Tympanic membrane, ossicles, oval window, perilymph wave, basilar membrane, stereocilia bending, hair cell depolarization, cochlear nerve firing
Tympanic membrane, ossicles, round window, endolymph wave, tectorial membrane, hair cell depolarization, cochlear nerve firing
Tympanic membrane, oval window, ossicles, perilymph wave, basilar membrane, stereocilia bending, hair cell hyperpolarization, cochlear nerve firing
Ossicles, tympanic membrane, oval window, basilar membrane, stereocilia bending, hair cell depolarization, cochlear nerve firing
cards.explanation: Each step drives the next: air moves the membrane, the membrane moves the bones, the stapes moves the fluid, the fluid moves the basilar membrane, that movement shears the stereocilia against the tectorial membrane, K+ entry depolarizes the hair cell, and glutamate release drives the cochlear nerve. Putting the oval window before the ossicles, or the ossicles before the eardrum, breaks the mechanical chain. Entry through the round window reverses the pressure relief point, and hair cell hyperpolarization would reduce rather than increase nerve firing.

cards.q: In otosclerosis the stapes becomes fixed to the oval window and can no longer move freely. Predict what happens to the traveling wave and to hearing.
cards.a: Little energy reaches the perilymph, so the wave is weak although hair cells are healthy.
options: The traveling wave shifts toward the apex, so only the high frequencies are still audible
Little energy reaches the perilymph, so the wave is weak although hair cells are healthy
Hair cells are destroyed by the extra pressure, causing permanent loss
The round window compensates fully, so hearing stays normal
cards.explanation: A fixed stapes cannot transfer vibration into the cochlear fluid, so the problem is delivery of energy rather than detection, and the cochlea and nerve remain intact. That is the definition of a conductive loss, and it is why bone conduction, which bypasses the ossicles entirely, still works well in these patients. Nothing here shifts the tuning of the membrane, the fixation reduces pressure transfer instead of raising it, and the round window cannot push fluid on its own.

cards.q: A drug selectively destroys outer hair cells while leaving inner hair cells and the cochlear nerve intact. Predict the effect on hearing.
cards.a: Loud sounds are still heard, but sensitivity and frequency sharpness are reduced.
options: Hearing is lost completely, since outer hair cells make most of the afferent synapses
Hearing is unchanged, since outer hair cells serve balance rather than hearing
Only loudness coding fails, while faint sounds are heard normally
Loud sounds are still heard, but sensitivity and frequency sharpness are reduced
cards.explanation: Outer hair cells change length in step with the traveling wave and amplify it, so losing them costs roughly 40 to 50 decibels of sensitivity and blurs the sharp tuning at each place, but the inner hair cells that actually report sound are still connected. Patients hear loud speech but struggle with faint sound and with separating similar frequencies. Inner hair cells, not outer, carry most afferent synapses, and outer hair cells belong to the cochlea rather than the vestibular apparatus.

cards.q: Two pure tones have the same frequency but one is much louder. Compare where the basilar membrane peaks and what the auditory nerve does.
cards.a: The peak is at the same place for both, and the louder tone produces a higher firing rate.
options: The peak is at the same place for both, and the louder tone produces a higher firing rate
The peak moves toward the base for the louder tone, and firing rate is unchanged
The peak moves toward the apex for the louder tone, and firing rate falls
The peaks are at different places and the firing rates are identical
cards.explanation: Place codes pitch and firing rate codes loudness, so two tones of the same frequency excite the same region and differ only in how strongly they drive it. The louder tone deflects the membrane further, opens more channels, and adds recruitment of nearby fibers. Any answer that moves the peak with intensity confuses the two codes, and identical firing rates would leave the brain no way to tell the two tones apart.

cards.q: Where is the lesion in a conductive hearing loss?
cards.a: In the outer or middle ear.
options: In the cochlear hair cells
In the outer or middle ear
In the cochlear nerve
In the auditory cortex
cards.explanation: Conductive loss means sound energy is not reaching the cochlea, so the fault lies in the ear canal, the tympanic membrane, or the ossicular chain. The cochlea and nerve are working normally, which is why bone conduction still delivers sound well. Hair cell and nerve lesions define sensorineural loss, and a cortical lesion causes trouble interpreting sound rather than a simple threshold shift.

cards.q: Where is the lesion in a sensorineural hearing loss?
cards.a: In the cochlea or the cochlear nerve.
options: In the ear canal
In the cochlea or the cochlear nerve
In the ossicular chain of the middle ear
In the tympanic membrane
cards.explanation: Sensorineural loss means the sound arrives but cannot be transduced or transmitted, so the problem is at the hair cells, the spiral ganglion, or CN VIII. Because the delivery system is intact, no route of delivery helps, and both air and bone conduction are reduced. The canal, eardrum, and ossicles are all parts of the conducting apparatus, so lesions there produce conductive loss instead.

cards.q: In a person with normal hearing, how do air conduction and bone conduction compare on the Rinne test?
cards.a: Air conduction is heard longer and louder than bone conduction.
