options: Bone conduction is heard longer than air conduction
Neither is heard once the fork stops touching the skull
The two are heard for exactly the same duration
Air conduction is heard longer and louder than bone conduction
cards.explanation: The middle ear amplifies airborne sound, so an intact conducting system makes air conduction the more efficient route, usually about twice as long. Bone conduction exceeding air conduction is the abnormal pattern that flags a conductive block. Equal durations would mean the middle ear is adding nothing, and sound presented at the ear canal is clearly heard without any skull contact.

cards.q: In the Weber test, a patient with a conductive loss in one ear hears the tone where?
cards.a: Louder in the affected ear.
options: Equally in both ears
Louder in the normal ear
Louder in the affected ear
Only when the fork touches the affected mastoid
cards.explanation: The bone conducted tone reaches both cochleas, and in the blocked ear the sound is not lost back out through the middle ear and is not competing with room noise, so it seems louder on that side. Lateralization to the better ear is the sensorineural pattern instead. Equal loudness is the normal result, and the Weber fork is placed on the midline of the skull rather than on one mastoid.

cards.q: In the Weber test, a patient with a sensorineural loss in one ear hears the tone where?
cards.a: Louder in the unaffected ear.
options: Louder in the affected ear
Equally in both ears
Not at all, in either ear
Louder in the unaffected ear
cards.explanation: Bone conduction delivers the tone equally to both inner ears, but the damaged cochlea cannot report it well, so the sound is perceived on the healthy side. Lateralizing to the bad ear would mean the inner ear is working and something is blocking delivery, which is the conductive pattern. Equal loudness is normal, and one damaged cochlea does not stop the other from hearing.

cards.q: Which of these is a typical cause of conductive hearing loss?
cards.a: Fluid in the middle ear from otitis media.
options: Fluid in the middle ear from otitis media
Prolonged exposure to loud machinery
An ototoxic antibiotic that kills hair cells
A tumor pressing on the cochlear nerve
cards.explanation: Middle ear fluid damps the ossicles and keeps the tympanic membrane from vibrating freely, so less energy reaches the oval window while the cochlea remains healthy. Noise exposure and ototoxic drugs destroy hair cells, and a nerve tumor interrupts transmission, so all three of those produce sensorineural loss. The distinguishing question is always whether the trouble is delivery or detection.

cards.q: Which of these is a typical cause of sensorineural hearing loss?
cards.a: Loss of cochlear hair cells after years of loud noise.
options: Loss of cochlear hair cells after years of loud noise
Perforation of the tympanic membrane
A plug of cerumen filling the ear canal
Fixation of the stapes against the oval window by new bone growth
cards.explanation: Hair cells do not regenerate in humans, so noise damage is permanent and lies inside the cochlea, which makes it sensorineural. Cerumen, a perforated eardrum, and a fixed stapes all interfere with getting vibration to the cochlea while leaving the sensory cells intact, so each of those is conductive. Sorting causes by anatomical location is the fastest way to keep the two categories straight.

cards.q: What Rinne result is expected in the affected ear of a patient with a conductive loss?
cards.a: Bone conduction is heard longer than air conduction.
options: Air conduction is heard longer than bone conduction
Bone conduction is heard longer than air conduction
Neither air nor bone conduction is heard
Both are heard, and both are longer than normal
cards.explanation: A blocked middle ear removes the amplification that normally makes air conduction superior, while bone conduction goes straight to a healthy cochlea and is unaffected, so the usual relationship reverses. That reversal is the single most useful sign that a loss is conductive. Preserved air over bone conduction with both reduced is the sensorineural pattern, and a conductive loss rarely abolishes hearing altogether.

cards.q: A child has had persistent middle ear fluid for weeks and now fails a hearing screen. How is this loss classified and why?
cards.a: Conductive, because the fluid blocks transfer of vibration to the oval window.
options: Sensorineural, because fluid pressure damages the hair cells
Conductive, because the fluid blocks transfer of vibration to the oval window
Sensorineural, because inflammation reaches the cochlear nerve
Mixed, because the tympanic membrane and cochlea are both involved
cards.explanation: Fluid loads the eardrum and ossicles so they cannot vibrate freely, which is a delivery problem in the middle ear and therefore conductive by definition. The cochlea is untouched, which is why hearing usually returns fully when the fluid clears. Calling it sensorineural would require damage to hair cells or nerve, and nothing in a simple effusion involves the cochlea.

cards.q: A patient develops hearing loss after several weeks of an aminoglycoside antibiotic known to kill cochlear hair cells. How is this loss classified?
cards.a: Sensorineural, because the transducing cells themselves are lost.
options: Conductive, because the drug thickens middle ear secretions
Sensorineural, because the transducing cells themselves are lost
Conductive, because hair cell loss stiffens the basilar membrane
Neither, because drug effects on hearing are always temporary
cards.explanation: The sound still reaches the cochlea normally, but with hair cells destroyed there is nothing left to convert the traveling wave into a receptor potential, which places the lesion in the sensory apparatus. Because human hair cells do not regenerate, this loss is usually permanent. Neither the middle ear nor basilar membrane stiffness is affected by the drug, so no part of this is conductive.

cards.q: A patient has a conductive loss in the right ear only. Predict the Weber result.
cards.a: The tone lateralizes to the right ear.
options: The tone lateralizes to the left ear
The tone is not heard on either side
The tone is heard equally in both ears
The tone lateralizes to the right ear
cards.explanation: With a healthy cochlea on both sides, the bone conducted tone is detected equally well, but the blocked right middle ear keeps the sound from leaking back out and shields that ear from background noise, so the tone seems louder on the blocked side. Lateralizing away from the affected ear would mean that cochlea was damaged, which is the sensorineural pattern. A one sided problem of either type rarely gives a midline result.

cards.q: A patient has a sensorineural loss in the left ear only. Predict the Rinne result on that side.
cards.a: Air conduction still outlasts bone conduction, but both are reduced.
options: Air conduction still outlasts bone conduction, but both are reduced
Bone conduction is heard longer than air conduction on the affected side
Air and bone conduction are both normal in duration
Only bone conduction is heard at all
cards.explanation: The middle ear is intact, so it still amplifies airborne sound better than the skull transmits it, and the normal air over bone relationship survives even though the damaged cochlea raises the threshold for both routes. That is why the Rinne alone can look deceptively normal in a sensorineural loss and must be read alongside the Weber. Bone conduction beating air conduction requires a conductive block, and truly normal durations would mean no loss at all.

cards.q: Why does bone conduction remain normal in a purely conductive hearing loss?
cards.a: Vibration passes through the skull straight to the cochlea, bypassing the blocked pathway.
options: The skull amplifies sound more than the ossicles do
Vibration passes through the skull straight to the cochlea, bypassing the blocked pathway
Bone conducted sound enters through the round window instead of the oval window
The cochlea becomes more sensitive when air conduction is reduced
cards.explanation: Bone conduction sets the whole temporal bone and the cochlear fluid in motion directly, so whatever is wrong in the canal, eardrum, or ossicles is simply skipped, and a healthy cochlea responds normally. This is the physical basis of every tuning fork test. The skull is actually a less efficient route than the middle ear in a normal ear, and the cochlea does not raise its own sensitivity to compensate.

cards.q: Which single finding best separates a conductive loss from a sensorineural loss in the same ear?
cards.a: Whether bone conduction exceeds air conduction in that ear.
options: Whether the loss is worse for high frequencies than for low
Whether the loss came on suddenly or gradually
Whether the patient also reports ringing in the ear
Whether bone conduction exceeds air conduction in that ear
cards.explanation: Comparing the two delivery routes isolates the question of whether sound is getting in, which is exactly the difference between the two categories, and only a conductive block reverses the normal air over bone relationship. High frequency predominance, tinnitus, and speed of onset are all common in sensorineural loss but occur in conductive cases too, so none of them decides the question on its own.

cards.q: On testing, the Weber tone lateralizes to the right ear, the right Rinne shows bone conduction longer than air conduction, and the left Rinne is normal. What is the diagnosis?
cards.a: A conductive loss in the right ear.
options: A sensorineural loss in the right ear
A sensorineural loss in the left ear
A conductive loss in the right ear
A conductive loss in the left ear
cards.explanation: Two findings point the same way: the reversed Rinne on the right says sound is not getting through that middle ear, and the Weber lateralizing toward that same ear says the cochlea underneath is healthy. Taken together only a right sided conductive block fits. A right sensorineural loss would send the Weber to the left and leave the right Rinne in its normal order. Nothing in the results implicates the left ear, whose Rinne is normal.

cards.q: On testing, the Weber tone lateralizes to the left ear while both ears show air conduction longer than bone conduction. What is the diagnosis?
cards.a: A sensorineural loss in the right ear.
options: A conductive loss in the left ear
A sensorineural loss in the left ear
A conductive loss in the right ear
A sensorineural loss in the right ear
cards.explanation: Normal Rinne results on both sides rule out a conductive block, so any hearing loss present must be sensorineural, and lateralization to the left means the left cochlea is the better one, placing the damage on the right. Reading the Weber without the Rinne is what leads students to name the wrong side here. A left sided lesion of either type would send the tone away from the left, and a conductive loss would have reversed a Rinne.

cards.q: A machinist with 25 years of unprotected noise exposure reports gradual hearing loss, worst for high pitched sounds. Predict both tuning fork results and name the type.
cards.a: Weber lateralizes to the better ear, Rinne stays air over bone in both ears, and the loss is sensorineural.
options: Weber lateralizes to the worse ear, Rinne is reversed there, and the loss is conductive
Weber lateralizes to the worse ear, Rinne stays air over bone in both ears, and the loss is sensorineural
Weber is midline, Rinne is reversed in both ears, and the loss is conductive
Weber lateralizes to the better ear, Rinne stays air over bone in both ears, and the loss is sensorineural
cards.explanation: Noise destroys hair cells at the base of the cochlea, which is a sensory lesion, so the middle ear still amplifies normally and the Rinne keeps its usual air over bone order in both ears. Because the damaged cochlea reports bone conducted sound poorly, the Weber goes to the healthier side. Any reversed Rinne would signal a conductive block that noise exposure does not cause, and lateralization toward a damaged cochlea contradicts how the Weber works.

cards.q: A patient perforated the right tympanic membrane during a diving accident. Predict the site of the problem, the loss type, and the Weber result.
cards.a: Middle ear delivery is impaired, the loss is conductive, and the Weber lateralizes to the right.
options: The cochlea is damaged, the loss is sensorineural, and the Weber lateralizes to the left
The cochlear nerve is stretched, the loss is sensorineural, and the Weber lateralizes to the right
Middle ear delivery is impaired, the loss is conductive, and the Weber lateralizes to the left
Middle ear delivery is impaired, the loss is conductive, and the Weber lateralizes to the right
cards.explanation: A hole in the eardrum means less of the sound pressure is collected and transferred to the ossicles, so this is a delivery failure in the conducting apparatus with an intact cochlea underneath. Since that cochlea works, the bone conducted Weber tone is heard best in the blocked ear, which is the right. Sending the Weber to the left would require the right cochlea to be the damaged one, and pressure injury to the eardrum does not by itself injure the nerve.

cards.q: Which vestibular structures detect rotational, or angular, acceleration of the head?
cards.a: The semicircular canals.
options: The tympanic cavity
The utricle and saccule
The cochlear duct
The semicircular canals
cards.explanation: The three semicircular canals are fluid filled loops, and rotating the head sets up relative motion of that fluid, which is only produced by a change in rotational speed. The utricle and saccule instead carry weighted membranes that respond to linear acceleration and to gravity. The cochlear duct handles hearing, and the tympanic cavity is the air filled middle ear.

cards.q: What is the cupula?
cards.a: The gelatinous cap in the ampulla that the hair cell stereocilia project into.
options: The calcium carbonate crystal layer of the macula
The gelatinous cap in the ampulla that the hair cell stereocilia project into
The bony wall of the semicircular canal
The membrane that separates perilymph from endolymph within the cochlear duct
cards.explanation: The cupula sits like a swinging door across the ampulla, and endolymph pushing on it bends the stereocilia embedded in its base. It has the same density as endolymph, which is why it responds to fluid motion but not to gravity. Calcium carbonate crystals belong to the otolithic membrane of the maculae, and the bony canal and cochlear membranes are structural rather than sensory elements.

cards.q: Where is the crista ampullaris located?
cards.a: In the ampulla of each semicircular canal.
options: In the wall of the utricle near the macula
In the ampulla of each semicircular canal
At the apex of the cochlear spiral
In the roof of the saccule near the macula
cards.explanation: Each canal widens into an ampulla, and the crista ampullaris is the ridge of hair cells and supporting cells inside it, topped by the cupula. Putting it in the utricle or saccule confuses it with the macula, the sensory patch of those two chambers. The cochlear apex belongs to hearing and contains no vestibular receptors.

cards.q: What sits on top of the hair cells in the macula of the utricle and saccule?
cards.a: A gel layer studded with calcium carbonate otoliths.
options: A cupula of the same density as endolymph
A thin sheet of stiff collagen with no added weight
A gel layer studded with calcium carbonate otoliths
A layer of endolymph secreting cells
cards.explanation: The otoliths make the overlying membrane denser than the fluid around it, so it lags behind during linear acceleration and slides downhill when the head tilts, dragging the stereocilia with it. Without that extra mass the structure could not sense gravity at all, which is exactly why the cupula, matched in density to endolymph, cannot. Secretory cells maintain endolymph composition but do not form the sensory covering.

cards.q: Which vestibular organ is best positioned to detect horizontal linear acceleration, such as a car pulling away from a stoplight?
cards.a: The utricle, whose macula lies roughly horizontally.
options: The utricle, whose macula lies roughly horizontally
The saccule, whose macula lies roughly vertically
The lateral semicircular canal
The cochlear duct
cards.explanation: A horizontal macula puts the otolithic membrane free to slide forward and back across the hair cells, so forward acceleration shears it in the plane that the utricle monitors. The saccular macula stands vertically and is better suited to up and down acceleration, such as an elevator start. Semicircular canals respond to rotation, not straight line motion, and the cochlear duct serves hearing.

cards.q: Which vestibular organ responds best to vertical acceleration, as when an elevator starts upward?
cards.a: The saccule.
options: The utricle
The posterior semicircular canal
The anterior semicircular canal
The saccule
cards.explanation: The saccular macula is oriented vertically, so up and down motion shears its otolithic membrane across the hair cells. The utricle, lying horizontally, is tuned to forward, backward, and sideways acceleration and to head tilt. The semicircular canals detect angular acceleration, so a straight ride up in an elevator barely stimulates them.

cards.q: Which cranial nerve carries equilibrium information from the vestibular apparatus?
cards.a: The vestibulocochlear nerve, CN VIII.
options: The trigeminal nerve, CN V
The vestibulocochlear nerve, CN VIII
The facial nerve, CN VII
The vagus nerve, CN X
cards.explanation: The vestibular branch of CN VIII carries afferents from the cristae and maculae to the vestibular nuclei in the brainstem and to the cerebellum. CN VII travels beside it in the temporal bone but is motor to facial muscles. CN V carries facial sensation, and CN X supplies thoracic and abdominal viscera, so neither is involved in balance.

cards.q: In a vestibular hair cell, what does bending of the stereocilia toward the tall kinocilium do?
cards.a: It depolarizes the cell and increases afferent firing.
options: It depolarizes the cell and increases afferent firing
It hyperpolarizes the cell and decreases afferent firing
It has no effect until the head stops moving
It closes all transduction channels at once
cards.explanation: Vestibular hair cells fire at a steady baseline rate, and deflection toward the kinocilium opens more transduction channels, depolarizes the cell, and raises that rate above baseline. Deflection away from the kinocilium does the opposite and drops firing below baseline, which is how one hair cell reports both directions of motion. Waiting until motion stops would make the system useless during movement, and total channel closure describes the opposite deflection.

cards.q: A person in a chair is spun rapidly to the right. What happens to the endolymph in the horizontal canals at the start of the spin?
cards.a: It lags behind the moving canal, so it pushes the cupula opposite to the turn.
options: It moves ahead of the canal wall and pulls the cupula forward
It stays perfectly still relative to the canal, so the cupula is not deflected
It lags behind the moving canal, so it pushes the cupula opposite to the turn
It drains toward the ampulla and increases pressure there
cards.explanation: The bony canal turns immediately with the head, but the fluid inside has inertia and is left behind, so relative to the canal wall it flows backward and deflects the cupula. That deflection bends the stereocilia and changes afferent firing, which is what signals the start of the turn. Fluid cannot lead the wall that is driving it, and if it moved perfectly with the canal there would be no stimulus at all. Endolymph is enclosed and does not drain.

cards.q: A person is spun at a constant speed for a full minute. What happens to the sensation of turning?
cards.a: It fades, because the endolymph catches up to the canal and the cupula returns to center.
options: It reverses, because the otoliths override the canal signal
It grows stronger, because hair cell firing accumulates over time
It stays constant, because the canals report the speed of rotation rather than acceleration
It fades, because the endolymph catches up to the canal and the cupula returns to center
cards.explanation: Friction brings the endolymph up to the same speed as the canal within about 20 seconds, and once nothing is shearing the cupula it springs back to its resting position and firing returns to baseline. This is why the semicircular canals report changes in rotation rather than steady rotation. Firing does not accumulate, the canals are acceleration detectors by design, and the otoliths respond to linear motion and cannot reverse a rotational signal.

cards.q: A person tilts the head to the right and holds it there. What happens in the utricle?
cards.a: Gravity pulls the heavy otolithic membrane sideways, shifting hair cell firing.
options: The endolymph in the utricle circulates and bends the cupula
Firing returns to baseline within seconds, because the tilt is not accelerating
Gravity pulls the heavy otolithic membrane sideways, shifting hair cell firing
The saccule alone responds, since the utricle detects only rotation
cards.explanation: Because the otolithic membrane is denser than its surroundings, gravity keeps pulling it downhill for as long as the tilt is held, so the shear on the stereocilia and the change in firing persist and report static head position. The canals, by contrast, adapt within seconds and cannot report a maintained position. The utricle has a macula rather than a cupula, and it responds to linear force and tilt, not rotation.

cards.q: Why are there three semicircular canals on each side rather than one?
cards.a: They lie in three perpendicular planes, so rotation about any axis is detected.
options: Each one is tuned to a different speed of rotation
They lie in three perpendicular planes, so rotation about any axis is detected
Two of them detect rotation while the third detects linear acceleration and head tilt
Each one drains endolymph from a different part of the labyrinth
cards.explanation: Any rotation can be broken into components about three axes, so a set of canals in three perpendicular planes can encode a head turn in any direction by how strongly each is stimulated. Nodding, shaking, and tilting the head each favor a different canal. They are not speed tuned, none of them detects linear motion, and the labyrinth is a closed system rather than a drainage network.

cards.q: An astronaut in orbit experiences apparent weightlessness. What happens to the vestibular signals?
cards.a: The maculae stop reporting tilt, while the canals still report head rotation.
options: Both the maculae and the canals stop working entirely
The canals stop reporting rotation, while the maculae still report head tilt normally
The maculae stop reporting tilt, while the canals still report head rotation
Both systems work normally, since neither depends on gravity
cards.explanation: The maculae work by letting a dense otolithic membrane be pulled by gravity or by linear acceleration, and in free fall there is no such pull, so tilt information disappears. The canals depend on fluid inertia during angular acceleration, which does not require gravity, so turning the head still produces a normal signal. The mismatch between a working canal signal and a silent otolith signal is a major source of space motion sickness.

cards.q: A patient has lost hair cell function in both maculae but has intact semicircular canals. Which task will be hardest?
cards.a: Sensing which way is up with the eyes closed.
options: Detecting the start of a head turn to the left
Hearing a conversation in a quiet room
Sensing which way is up with the eyes closed
Judging the pitch of a musical note
cards.explanation: Static head orientation relative to gravity is reported by the otolith organs, so losing them removes the internal sense of upright, and without vision to substitute the patient becomes disoriented. The onset of a head turn is a job for the canals, which are intact here. Hearing and pitch discrimination belong to the cochlea, a separate part of the inner ear that this lesion does not touch.

cards.q: A dancer spins to the right and then stops abruptly. Immediately after stopping, what does she sense and why?
cards.a: A sensation of spinning to the left, because the endolymph keeps moving past the cupula.
options: Nothing, because the cupula returns to center as soon as motion stops
A sensation of falling, because the otoliths are displaced by the stop
A stronger sensation of spinning to the right, because hair cell firing rebounds above baseline
A sensation of spinning to the left, because the endolymph keeps moving past the cupula
cards.explanation: By the end of the spin the endolymph had matched the head's rotation, so when the head stops the fluid keeps going by inertia and deflects the cupula in the direction opposite to the original deflection. The brain reads that as rotation the other way, which is the dizziness felt after spinning. The cupula cannot recenter instantly while fluid is still moving, and the sensation is reversed rather than intensified. The otoliths report linear force and are not the source of this illusion.

cards.q: A passenger sits facing forward in a train that accelerates smoothly ahead on straight, level track with the head held still. Trace which receptors respond.
cards.a: The utricular macula responds, while the semicircular canals stay near baseline.
options: The horizontal semicircular canals respond, while the maculae stay near baseline
The saccular macula responds, while the utricle stays near baseline
Both the canals and both maculae respond equally
The utricular macula responds, while the semicircular canals stay near baseline
cards.explanation: Forward acceleration is linear and horizontal, so the dense otolithic membrane of the horizontally oriented utricle lags and shears the hair cells beneath it. There is no change in rotation, so the endolymph in the canals stays with its walls and the cupulae are not deflected. The saccule is oriented for vertical motion, so it contributes little on level track.

cards.q: A patient reports that turning the head produces violent spinning sensations, while standing still with the eyes closed feels normal. Which part of the vestibular apparatus is most likely at fault?
cards.a: The semicircular canals, which report angular acceleration.
options: The semicircular canals, which report angular acceleration
The saccule, which reports vertical linear acceleration
The utricle, which reports horizontal linear acceleration
The cochlear duct, which reports sound
cards.explanation: The symptom appears only during rotation and disappears when the head is still, which matches the stimulus the canals are built to detect and rules out an organ that would misreport gravity even at rest. Otolith disease tends to produce a persistent sense of tilt or unsteadiness while standing, which this patient does not have. The cochlear duct handles hearing and would produce hearing loss or tinnitus instead of vertigo.

cards.q: A person leans backward in a reclining chair and holds the position, then quickly nods the head forward and back. Which receptors are active at each stage?
cards.a: The maculae signal the maintained lean, and the canals fire during the nodding.
options: The canals signal the maintained lean, and the maculae fire during the nodding
The maculae signal the maintained lean, and the canals fire during the nodding
The maculae handle both stages, since the canals respond only to spinning
The canals handle both stages, since the maculae respond only to sound
cards.explanation: A held lean is a static orientation to gravity, exactly what the weighted otolithic membranes of the utricle and saccule report and continue to report as long as the position lasts. Nodding is angular acceleration in the vertical plane, so it deflects the cupula in the canals aligned with that plane and the response fades if the motion becomes steady. Swapping the two organs misses that one adapts quickly and the other does not, and the maculae play no role in hearing.

cards.q: What are the five basic taste qualities?
cards.a: Sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and umami.
options: Sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and spicy
Sweet, salty, bitter, umami, and fatty
Sweet, sour, salty, metallic, and umami
Sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and umami
cards.explanation: Each of the five has its own receptor mechanism on the taste cell, and umami, the savory taste of glutamate, was the last to be confirmed. Spiciness is not a taste at all but activation of pain and temperature endings by capsaicin through the trigeminal nerve. Metallic and fatty sensations are studied but are not among the established five.

cards.q: Which second messenger carries the olfactory signal inside an olfactory receptor neuron?
cards.a: Cyclic AMP.
options: Cyclic AMP
Cyclic GMP
Inositol trisphosphate
Diacylglycerol
cards.explanation: An odorant binds a G protein coupled receptor, Golf activates adenylyl cyclase, and the cyclic AMP produced opens cation channels directly. Cyclic GMP is the messenger in photoreceptors, where the light response closes channels instead of opening them. Inositol trisphosphate and diacylglycerol are messengers in other G protein pathways, including some taste transduction, but not in the main olfactory cascade.

cards.q: Which cranial nerve carries taste from the anterior two thirds of the tongue?
cards.a: The facial nerve, CN VII.
options: The facial nerve, CN VII
The glossopharyngeal nerve, CN IX
The trigeminal nerve, CN V
The vagus nerve, CN X
cards.explanation: Taste from the front of the tongue travels with CN VII, while CN IX carries taste from the posterior third and CN X picks up the few taste buds on the epiglottis and upper esophagus. CN V supplies general touch, temperature, and pain to the anterior tongue, which is why it carries the burn of chili but not the taste.

cards.q: Through which bony structure do olfactory receptor neuron axons pass on their way to the brain?
cards.a: The cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone.
options: The cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone
The optic canal of the sphenoid bone
The foramen magnum of the occipital bone
The internal acoustic meatus of the temporal bone
cards.explanation: The cribriform plate is perforated by many small holes, and bundles of unmyelinated olfactory axons thread through them to reach the olfactory bulb sitting just above. That thin, perforated bone is also why a blow to the head can shear the axons and abolish smell. The optic canal transmits CN II, the internal acoustic meatus transmits CN VII and CN VIII, and the foramen magnum transmits the spinal cord.

cards.q: Where do olfactory receptor neurons first synapse?
cards.a: In the glomeruli of the olfactory bulb.
options: In the glomeruli of the olfactory bulb
In the solitary nucleus of the medulla
In the ventral posteromedial nucleus of the thalamus
In the piriform cortex of the temporal lobe
cards.explanation: Receptor neurons expressing the same odorant receptor converge on the same glomerulus, where they synapse on mitral cells, and that sorting is the first step in coding which odorant is present. The solitary nucleus is the first relay for taste, not smell. The ventral posteromedial nucleus is the thalamic taste relay, and the piriform cortex receives olfactory information only after the bulb has processed it.

cards.q: What is unusual about the olfactory pathway compared with the other special senses?
cards.a: It reaches cortex and limbic areas without a thalamic relay first.
options: Its receptors are modified muscle cells rather than neurons
It has no receptor cells and senses chemicals directly through the mucosa
It sends all of its output to the opposite side of the brain
It reaches cortex and limbic areas without a thalamic relay first
cards.explanation: Vision, hearing, taste, and body sensation all pass through a thalamic nucleus before reaching cortex, but the olfactory tract runs directly to piriform cortex, amygdala, and entorhinal cortex, with the thalamic route to orbitofrontal cortex added afterward. Olfactory receptor neurons are true bipolar neurons and are the receptor cells themselves, and most olfactory projections stay on the same side.

cards.q: A salty solution and a bitter compound both reach the tongue. How do their transduction mechanisms differ?
cards.a: Salt enters taste cells directly through ion channels, while bitter acts through a G protein coupled receptor.
options: Salt enters taste cells directly through ion channels, while bitter acts through a G protein coupled receptor
Both act through G protein coupled receptors, but on different cell types
Bitter enters taste cells directly through ion channels, while salt acts through a G protein coupled receptor
Both enter directly through ion channels, but salt uses Na+ and bitter uses K+
cards.explanation: Na+ from a salty solution flows straight into the taste cell through membrane channels and depolarizes it, which is the simplest transduction mechanism in the body, and sour works similarly through H+. Sweet, bitter, and umami all bind receptors on the cell surface and work through gustducin and a second messenger cascade. Swapping the two mechanisms is the common error here, and no taste is transduced by K+ entry.

cards.q: An odorant binds its receptor and cyclic AMP rises inside the olfactory receptor neuron. What happens next to the membrane?
cards.a: Cation channels open, positive charge flows in, and the neuron depolarizes.
options: Cation channels close, positive current stops, and the neuron hyperpolarizes
Cl- channels open and the neuron is inhibited
Cation channels open, positive charge flows in, and the neuron depolarizes
The neuron releases transmitter without any change in membrane potential
cards.explanation: The cyclic AMP gated channels of olfactory neurons open when the messenger rises, so the stimulus produces an inward cation current, a depolarizing receptor potential, and if it is large enough, action potentials along the axon into the bulb. That is the ordinary pattern for a sensory receptor. Channel closure with hyperpolarization describes photoreceptors, which are the exception, and nothing in the cascade opens Cl- channels or releases transmitter independent of voltage.

cards.q: Why does a familiar smell so often trigger an emotional memory before you can name the odor?
cards.a: Olfactory axons reach the amygdala and entorhinal cortex directly, ahead of any naming pathway.
options: Olfactory receptors are located within the limbic system itself
Odor molecules cross into the blood and act on the hippocampus as hormones
Olfactory axons reach the amygdala and entorhinal cortex directly, ahead of any naming pathway
Smell signals travel faster than other sensory signals because the axons are heavily myelinated
cards.explanation: The olfactory tract projects into limbic structures involved in emotion and memory without waiting for a thalamic relay, so the affective response can arrive before the slower route to areas that identify and name the odor. Receptor neurons sit in the nasal epithelium, not in the limbic system, and odorants act on receptors rather than circulating as hormones. Olfactory axons are in fact unmyelinated and slow, so speed is not the explanation.

cards.q: A patient with a heavy head cold says food tastes like nothing. Taste testing with salt and sugar solutions is normal. What explains the complaint?
cards.a: Flavor depends heavily on smell, and congestion blocks odorants from the epithelium.
options: The taste buds have been destroyed by the infection
Mucus changes the pH of saliva enough to silence the taste receptors
Flavor depends heavily on smell, and congestion blocks odorants from the epithelium
The facial nerve is inflamed, which abolishes taste from the whole surface of the tongue
cards.explanation: What we call the taste of food is mostly the odorant portion, sensed retronasally as we chew and swallow, so blocking airflow to the olfactory epithelium flattens flavor while the five basic tastes stay intact. That is exactly the pattern shown by normal salt and sugar testing. Destroyed taste buds or an inflamed CN VII would have made those test solutions abnormal too, and saliva pH shifts in a cold are far too small to silence receptors.

cards.q: Olfactory receptor neurons are unusual among neurons because they are replaced throughout life. Why is this necessary?
cards.a: They are directly exposed to the outside air and are regularly damaged.
options: They must change their receptor type as the diet changes
They use up their odorant receptors permanently with each binding event
They are directly exposed to the outside air and are regularly damaged
They are destroyed by every action potential they fire
cards.explanation: These neurons place their cilia in the mucus of the nasal cavity, where dust, pathogens, and dry air reach them, so a basal stem cell population replaces them every month or two, and each new neuron must grow an axon back to the correct glomerulus. Receptors are proteins that release the odorant and are reused, cells do not switch receptor types with diet, and firing an action potential does not destroy a neuron.

cards.q: Compare the effect of the stimulus on the ion channels of an olfactory receptor neuron and a photoreceptor.
cards.a: Odorant opens cyclic AMP gated channels and depolarizes, while light closes cyclic GMP gated channels and hyperpolarizes.
options: Both stimuli open cyclic nucleotide gated channels and both cells depolarize
Odorant closes cyclic AMP gated channels and hyperpolarizes, while light opens cyclic GMP gated channels and depolarizes
Odorant opens cyclic AMP gated channels and depolarizes, while light closes cyclic GMP gated channels and hyperpolarizes
Both stimuli close cyclic nucleotide gated channels, but only the photoreceptor hyperpolarizes
cards.explanation: Both cells use a cyclic nucleotide gated cation channel, but the cascades push the messenger in opposite directions: odorant binding raises cyclic AMP and opens channels, while light activates a phosphodiesterase that destroys cyclic GMP and lets channels shut. The result is a depolarizing receptor potential in the nose and a hyperpolarizing one in the retina. Treating the two the same misses the point that vision is the exception among the senses, and reversing them assigns each cell the other one's behavior.

cards.q: Trace an odorant molecule from the nasal cavity to conscious perception. Which sequence is correct?
cards.a: Odorant binds cilia of a receptor neuron, the axon passes the cribriform plate to a glomerulus, mitral cells project through the olfactory tract to piriform cortex and amygdala.
options: Odorant binds cilia of a receptor neuron, the axon passes the cribriform plate to a glomerulus, mitral cells project through the olfactory tract to piriform cortex and amygdala
Odorant binds cilia of a receptor neuron, the axon synapses first in the thalamus, and thalamic neurons then project to the olfactory bulb and on to the piriform cortex
Odorant binds a supporting cell, which excites a receptor neuron, whose axon runs to the solitary nucleus and then to the insula
Odorant binds cilia of a receptor neuron, the axon runs to the olfactory bulb, and bulb neurons project first to the occipital cortex
cards.explanation: The receptor neuron itself sends its axon through the cribriform plate into the bulb, where it synapses in a glomerulus on mitral cells, and the mitral cell axons form the tract that reaches cortex and limbic targets directly. Routing the signal through the thalamus first, or through the solitary nucleus and insula, describes the taste pathway rather than smell. Supporting cells maintain the epithelium and do not transduce, and the occipital cortex is visual.

cards.q: After a fall, a patient can taste salt and sugar normally but cannot smell coffee or identify foods by flavor. Imaging shows an injury at the base of the frontal region. What was most likely damaged and why does flavor suffer?
cards.a: The olfactory axons crossing the cribriform plate, and flavor depends largely on the olfactory component.
options: The facial nerve, and flavor suffers because taste buds have lost their innervation
The thalamic taste relay, and flavor suffers because all chemical senses pass through the thalamus
The solitary nucleus, and flavor suffers because taste and smell are relayed together there
The olfactory axons crossing the cribriform plate, and flavor depends largely on the olfactory component
cards.explanation: Preserved responses to salt and sugar show the taste pathway is intact, so the deficit must be olfactory, and unmyelinated axons crossing a thin perforated bone are the part of that pathway most easily sheared by head trauma. Because most of what people call flavor is the smell of food sensed while chewing, losing smell alone flattens meals. A CN VII, solitary nucleus, or thalamic taste lesion would each have degraded the salt and sugar testing, which was normal here.

cards.q: At what distance is a standard Snellen chart read during acuity testing?
cards.a: 20 feet, or about 6 meters.
options: 10 feet, or about 3 meters
14 inches, or about 35 centimeters
20 feet, or about 6 meters
At whatever distance the letters first become clear
cards.explanation: Twenty feet is treated as optical infinity, so the rays arriving at the eye are essentially parallel and no accommodation is needed, which is what makes the measurement a clean test of distance vision. Fourteen inches is the standard distance for a handheld near card, which tests a different thing. Ten feet is used only with a mirror system that doubles the path, and letting the subject choose the distance would make results impossible to compare.

cards.q: What does a Snellen result of 20/20 mean?
cards.a: At 20 feet the subject reads what a normal eye reads at 20 feet.
options: The subject read 20 letters correctly out of the 20 that were tried
The subject sees 20 percent better than average
At 20 feet the subject reads what a normal eye reads at 20 feet
The subject's near point is 20 centimeters
cards.explanation: The top number is the subject's testing distance and the bottom number is the distance at which a normal eye could read that same line, so matching numbers means normal acuity. Counting letters correct is not how the fraction is built. The fraction is not a percentage of normal, and the near point is measured by a separate accommodation test.

cards.q: What do Ishihara plates test?
cards.a: Color vision, especially red and green discrimination.
options: Visual acuity at near
The size and position of the blind spot in each eye
Color vision, especially red and green discrimination
The near point of accommodation for each eye separately
cards.explanation: Each plate hides a number in dots that differ from the background only in hue, so a subject who cannot distinguish those hues reads no figure or a different one. The plates are designed mainly around the red and green confusions produced by the common cone pigment deficiencies. Acuity, blind spot mapping, and near point each have their own test in the lab.

cards.q: What is the approximate near point of accommodation for a healthy young adult?
cards.a: About 10 centimeters.
options: About 1 centimeter
About 1 meter
About 50 centimeters
About 10 centimeters
cards.explanation: A young elastic lens can add enough power to keep an object sharp until it is roughly a hand's width from the eye, so about 10 cm is the expected result in the lab. One centimeter is far closer than any human lens can manage. Values near 50 cm or a meter are what you record in older subjects whose lenses have stiffened, so finding one in a 20 year old should prompt a repeat measurement.

cards.q: The blind spot found during the mapping exercise corresponds to which structure?
cards.a: The optic disc, where axons leave the eye.
options: The optic disc, where axons leave the eye
The fovea centralis, at the center of the macula
The macula lutea, around the fovea
The ora serrata, at the retinal edge
cards.explanation: No rods or cones can sit where the ganglion cell axons gather to form the optic nerve, so any image falling on that patch is not detected and the subject reports the target disappearing. The fovea and the surrounding macula are the region of best vision rather than a gap. The ora serrata is the peripheral edge of the retina and does not create a discrete spot in the field.

cards.q: Why is each eye tested separately during acuity and blind spot testing?
cards.a: Because the other eye would cover the deficit and hide the problem.
options: Because binocular testing overstimulates the retina and blurs the chart
Because the chart is only visible from one angle
Because the two eyes cannot accommodate at the same time
Because the other eye would cover the deficit and hide the problem
cards.explanation: Visual fields overlap heavily, so a defect in one eye is filled in by the other and a subject with a real deficit can score normally with both eyes open, which is exactly why the blind spot goes unnoticed in daily life. Covering one eye removes that compensation. Binocular viewing does not overstimulate anything, both eyes accommodate together, and the chart is meant to be read from straight ahead.

cards.q: An astigmatism chart shows lines radiating from a center point. What does a positive finding look like?
cards.a: Lines at some orientations look sharp while others look blurred.
options: Every line looks equally blurred
Lines at some orientations look sharp while others look blurred
The center point disappears entirely
The lines appear to bow outward, as though the chart were curved
cards.explanation: Astigmatism gives the eye two focal planes at right angles, so only the lines aligned with the plane that lands on the retina are crisp, and the rest are out of focus, which makes the pattern look uneven around the clock. Uniform blur points to a spherical error such as myopia. A vanishing center suggests a central field defect, and bowing of lines suggests distortion at the macula rather than a refractive problem.

cards.q: How is the common form of red and green color deficiency inherited?
cards.a: As an X linked recessive trait, so it is far more common in males.
options: As an autosomal dominant trait affecting both sexes equally
As an X linked recessive trait, so it is far more common in males
As a mitochondrial trait passed only from the mother to all children
It is not inherited and results from retinal injury
cards.explanation: The genes for the long and medium wavelength cone pigments sit on the X chromosome, so a male with one affected X has no second copy to compensate, which is why roughly 8 percent of males and under 1 percent of females are affected. An autosomal dominant pattern would give equal rates in both sexes. Mitochondrial inheritance would affect all children of an affected mother, and while injury can damage color vision, the common deficiencies are genetic.

cards.q: A subject reads only the line marked 20/50 on the chart. How is this interpreted?
cards.a: Acuity is worse than normal, since a normal eye could read that line from 50 feet.
options: Acuity is better than normal, since more letters were read than expected
The result cannot be interpreted without knowing the subject's age
Acuity is normal, since the subject was 20 feet from the chart
Acuity is worse than normal, since a normal eye could read that line from 50 feet
cards.explanation: The subject must come in to 20 feet to see what an ordinary eye resolves from 50 feet away, so detail is lost and acuity is reduced. A larger bottom number always means worse acuity, which is the reverse of most scoring systems and is the usual source of confusion. Standing at 20 feet is simply the protocol, and the fraction is interpreted the same way at any age.

cards.q: A subject reads the 20/15 line correctly. What does this indicate?
cards.a: Acuity is better than average, since a normal eye must come to 15 feet.
options: Acuity is worse than average, because the smaller number means less detail
Acuity is better than average, since a normal eye must come to 15 feet
The subject stood 15 feet from the chart instead of 20
The result is invalid, because 20/20 is the best possible score
cards.explanation: The subject is resolving from 20 feet what an average eye needs to approach to 15 feet to see, so the eye is doing better than the reference standard, and results down to about 20/10 are seen in healthy young subjects. The bottom number describes the reference eye, not the subject's position. Because 20/20 is an average rather than a ceiling, better scores are perfectly valid.

cards.q: A 48-year-old subject has a measured near point of 33 centimeters. How should this be interpreted?
cards.a: It is consistent with presbyopia, since the near point recedes as the lens stiffens.
options: It is normal for any adult, since the near point does not change with age
It indicates myopia, since the eye focuses too strongly at near
It is consistent with presbyopia, since the near point recedes as the lens stiffens
It indicates a paralyzed ciliary muscle, since accommodation has failed completely
cards.explanation: The near point moves steadily outward from about 10 cm in youth to a third of a meter or more by the late forties, so this value fits the expected age related change in lens elasticity rather than any disease. Myopia would move the near point closer, not farther away. Complete ciliary paralysis would push the near point out to optical infinity and would also blur near vision through any correction.

cards.q: A subject misreads several Ishihara plates but has 20/20 acuity in both eyes. Where does the problem most likely lie?
cards.a: In the cone photopigments, which affects hue discrimination but not resolution.
options: In the cornea, which is scattering light of certain wavelengths
In the cone photopigments, which affects hue discrimination but not resolution
In the lens, which has lost the elasticity needed to focus fine detail
In the optic tract, which is carrying only half of each visual field
cards.explanation: Sharp acuity proves that the optics and the foveal cone mosaic are resolving fine detail normally, so the failure has to be in which pigments those cones carry rather than in focus. A missing or shifted pigment collapses two hues into one, which is exactly what the plates are designed to expose. Corneal and lens problems would blur the letters as well, and an optic tract lesion would remove half of the visual field rather than confuse colors.

cards.q: During blind spot mapping the right eye fixates on a central mark and the target disappears when it is moved to the right. Why does the blind spot appear on that side of the field?
cards.a: The optic disc lies nasal to the fovea, and the nasal retina views the temporal field.
options: The optic disc lies temporal to the fovea, and the temporal retina views the temporal field
The blind spot can appear on either side depending on which hand holds the card
The optic disc lies directly behind the fovea, so the spot appears at the center
The optic disc lies nasal to the fovea, and the nasal retina views the temporal field
cards.explanation: Light crosses through the pupil, so a target in the temporal field lands on the nasal retina, and because the optic disc sits nasal to the fovea, the gap shows up out toward the temple, roughly 15 degrees from center. Placing the disc on the temporal side reverses the anatomy and would predict the spot on the wrong side. The disc is offset from the fovea rather than behind it, and the geometry does not depend on the examiner.

cards.q: Why does a subject never notice the blind spot while walking around, even though the lab test finds it easily?
cards.a: The other eye covers that part of the field, and the brain fills the gap.
options: The other eye covers that part of the field, and the brain fills the gap
The blind spot closes when both eyes are open
Constant eye movement keeps images off the optic disc at all times of day
The blind spot only exists under the bright light used in the lab
cards.explanation: The two blind spots fall on opposite sides of the field, so each eye supplies what the other misses, and even with one eye closed the visual system continues the surrounding texture across the gap so no hole is perceived. That is why the test requires covering one eye and fixating steadily. The optic disc is a permanent structural gap that does not close, and although the eyes do move, images still cross the disc constantly.

cards.q: A subject with glasses is asked to keep them on during acuity testing. What does the recorded result then describe?
cards.a: Corrected acuity, meaning how the eye performs with its error compensated.
options: Uncorrected acuity, which reflects the true optical state of the eye itself
The near point of accommodation for that subject
The strength of the prescription in diopters
Corrected acuity, meaning how the eye performs with its error compensated
cards.explanation: Testing through the usual correction answers the practical question of how well the person sees in daily life and separates retinal and neural function from a lens problem the glasses already solve. Removing the glasses would measure uncorrected acuity, which is a different and equally legitimate measurement as long as the record says which one was taken. A chart cannot report diopters, and the near point requires the accommodation test.

cards.q: A 50-year-old reads 20/20 at distance in each eye, passes every Ishihara plate, and has a near point of 45 centimeters. What is the interpretation?
cards.a: Distance acuity and color vision are normal, and the receded near point indicates presbyopia.
options: Distance acuity and color vision are normal, and the receded near point indicates presbyopia
All results are within normal limits for any adult
The normal chart result rules out any need for correction
The color plates and the receded near point together suggest cone loss in the central fovea
cards.explanation: Each test isolates a different function, and here two are normal while the third is not, so the deficit is specifically in accommodation rather than in the optics for distance or in the retina. A near point of 45 cm at this age is the expected consequence of a stiffened lens and predicts the need for a reading add. Calling everything normal ignores the near point, and normal color plates argue against foveal cone loss rather than for it.

cards.q: A subject reads only the 20/100 line without glasses but reads 20/20 with them. What does the pair of results establish?
cards.a: The retina and visual pathway are working, and the deficit is a refractive error.
options: The retina is damaged, since acuity was clearly poor on the first test without glasses
The retina and visual pathway are working, and the deficit is a refractive error
The subject has a color vision deficiency that the glasses mask
The near point must also be abnormal, since acuity was reduced
cards.explanation: A lens in front of the eye can only change where light focuses, so if a lens restores acuity to normal the photoreceptors and the pathway behind them must be intact and the original problem was optical. This comparison is the fastest way in the lab to separate a refractive error from retinal or neural disease. Glasses cannot compensate for missing cone pigments, and the near point is a separate measurement that may well be normal.

cards.q: A student maps the blind spot, then repeats the test holding the card twice as far from the eye. What happens to the measured gap on the card and why?
cards.a: The gap measures larger, because the same angle of field covers more distance farther away.
options: The gap disappears, because the target no longer falls on the optic disc
The gap measures smaller, because the optic disc always subtends a fixed number of centimeters
The gap is unchanged, because the blind spot is a fixed size on the card
The gap measures larger, because the same angle of field covers more distance farther away
cards.explanation: The blind spot is a fixed patch of retina, so it always blocks the same angle of the visual field, and an angle spreads over more centimeters the farther away the card is held. Doubling the distance therefore roughly doubles the measured width while the underlying anatomy is unchanged. Treating the spot as a fixed number of centimeters reverses the geometry, and moving the card farther away does not stop light from that direction landing on the disc.

cards.q: A 19-year-old has 20/20 acuity, a near point of 9 centimeters, and misses eight Ishihara plates. Where in the visual system does the fault lie, and what does the near point add?
cards.a: At the cone pigments in the retina, and the normal near point shows the optics work.
options: In the lens, and the near point confirms that it has already stiffened unusually early
At the cone pigments in the retina, and the normal near point shows the optics work
In the optic chiasm, and the near point is irrelevant to that lesion
In the ciliary muscle, and the color plates were probably misread
cards.explanation: Normal acuity and a normal near point together show that the cornea, lens, and ciliary muscle are delivering a sharp image at every distance, so nothing optical explains the color result, which leaves the pigments in the cones themselves. That combination is the expected profile of an inherited red and green deficiency in a young man. A stiffened lens would have pushed the near point out, and a chiasm lesion would have produced a field defect rather than color confusion.

cards.q: Where is the vibrating tuning fork placed to perform the Weber test?
cards.a: On the midline of the forehead or the top of the skull.
options: On the mastoid process behind one ear
On the midline of the forehead or the top of the skull
Just outside one ear canal without touching the head
On the angle of the jaw on the affected side
cards.explanation: A midline placement delivers the same bone conducted stimulus to both inner ears, which is the only way a difference in perceived loudness can be attributed to the ears rather than to the placement. Putting the fork on one mastoid tests bone conduction on that side and is the first half of the Rinne. Holding it beside the ear tests air conduction, and the jaw is not a standard site.

cards.q: What is the correct order of steps in the Rinne test?
cards.a: Place the fork on the mastoid until the tone fades, then hold it beside the ear canal.
options: Hold the fork beside the ear canal, and then press its base against the middle of the forehead
Hold the fork beside each ear in turn and compare left with right
Place the fork on both mastoids at once and compare the two sides
Place the fork on the mastoid until the tone fades, then hold it beside the ear canal
cards.explanation: The test compares bone conduction with air conduction in one ear, so the mastoid placement is timed first and the fork is then moved to the air route to see whether the tone returns. A normal ear still hears it, because the middle ear amplifies airborne sound. Comparing the two sides to each other is what the Weber does, and a forehead placement is the Weber technique rather than the Rinne.

cards.q: In tuning fork testing, what does lateralization mean?
cards.a: The tone is heard louder in one ear than the other.
options: Air conduction outlasts bone conduction in the same ear
The fork is moved from one side of the head to the other
The tone changes pitch as the fork slows down
The tone is heard louder in one ear than the other
cards.explanation: During the Weber test the sound reaches both cochleas equally, so if the subject reports it as louder on one side the result is said to lateralize to that side, and the direction is what identifies the type of loss. Moving the fork is a step in the procedure rather than a finding. A fading fork loses loudness but not pitch, and comparing air with bone conduction is the Rinne comparison.

cards.q: Which tuning fork frequency is standard for the Weber and Rinne tests?
options: 128 Hz
256 Hz
512 Hz
cards.explanation: A 512 Hz fork sits in the speech range and gives a tone that lasts long enough to time while still being carried well by air, which is why it is the clinical standard. Lower frequency forks such as 128 Hz are felt as vibration as much as heard, so subjects confuse touch with sound. Very high frequency forks fade too quickly for a reliable comparison.

cards.q: How should the tuning fork be set vibrating before testing?
cards.a: Struck gently against the heel of the hand or another soft surface.
options: Struck sharply against the hard edge of the lab bench or a metal table
Struck gently against the heel of the hand or another soft surface
Squeezed between the fingers and released
Tapped against the subject's mastoid process
cards.explanation: A soft strike produces a clean fundamental tone at a moderate intensity, which is what the comparison depends on. Striking a hard surface adds overtones and can start the tone so loud that a mild difference between the two routes is missed. Squeezing the tines produces almost no vibration, and striking the fork against the subject is uncomfortable and starts the test before the timing begins.

cards.q: How is the Romberg test performed?
cards.a: The subject stands with feet together, eyes open and then closed.
options: The subject sits in a rotating chair and is spun ten times
The subject walks heel to toe along a straight line with eyes open
The subject stands with feet together, eyes open and then closed
The subject stands on one leg while counting backward
cards.explanation: Narrowing the base of support and then removing vision isolates how much the subject depends on sight to stay upright, which is the point of the test. Tandem walking and single leg stance are other balance tasks but do not make the eyes open versus eyes closed comparison. The rotating chair is used to test the semicircular canals by producing nystagmus, which is a different procedure.

cards.q: What does closing the eyes remove during the Romberg test?
cards.a: Visual information about body position, leaving vestibular and proprioceptive input.
options: Vestibular input, leaving vision and proprioception
Visual information about body position, leaving vestibular and proprioceptive input
Proprioceptive input from the legs, leaving vision and the vestibular system
Cerebellar control of posture, leaving reflex balance only
cards.explanation: Balance normally draws on three streams, vision, the vestibular apparatus, and proprioception, and closing the eyes removes only the first, so any remaining steadiness depends on the other two. That is why a subject with a vestibular or proprioceptive deficit can look normal until the eyes close. Closing the eyes has no effect on the inner ear, on joint and muscle receptors, or on the cerebellum.

cards.q: What is nystagmus?
cards.a: A rhythmic eye movement with a slow drift and a quick jerk back.
options: A sustained deviation of both eyes toward one side of the visual field
A loss of the pupillary light reflex in one eye
A rhythmic eye movement with a slow drift and a quick jerk back
An inability to move the eyes past the midline
cards.explanation: The slow phase is driven by the vestibular signal and the quick phase is the brainstem resetting gaze, and their alternation makes the eyes appear to beat in one direction. Observing it after rotation shows that the canals and their brainstem connections are working. A fixed deviation, a lost pupillary reflex, and restricted eye movement each point to other problems, none of which involve the rhythmic pattern that defines nystagmus.

cards.q: During a Weber test a student plugs one ear tightly with a finger. What does the subject report and why?
cards.a: The tone sounds louder in the plugged ear, because the plug mimics a conductive block.
options: The tone sounds louder in the open ear, because that side is receiving more sound
The tone sounds louder in the plugged ear, because the plug mimics a conductive block
The tone becomes inaudible on both sides
The tone stays exactly midline, because a finger cannot change bone conduction
cards.explanation: Plugging the canal blocks the air route while leaving the cochlea untouched, which is precisely what a conductive loss does, so the bone conducted tone is not lost back out through the middle ear and is not competing with room noise on that side. Demonstrating this on yourself is the quickest way to remember which way the Weber lateralizes. Nothing about the plug reduces cochlear function or eliminates bone conduction, so the tone is neither shifted to the open ear nor lost.

cards.q: A subject's Weber tone lateralizes to the right ear and the right Rinne shows bone conduction outlasting air conduction. How is this recorded?
cards.a: A conductive loss on the right.
options: A sensorineural loss on the right
A conductive loss on the right
A conductive loss on the left
Normal hearing with a technique error
cards.explanation: Bone beating air on the right says the sound is not getting through that middle ear, and the Weber pointing to the same ear says the cochlea underneath is healthy, so the two findings agree on a right sided conductive block. A right sensorineural loss would send the Weber to the left and leave the Rinne in normal order. Nothing in the findings implicates the left ear, and consistent results across two tests argue against a technique error.

cards.q: A subject's Weber tone lateralizes to the left ear while both ears show air conduction outlasting bone conduction. How is this recorded?
cards.a: A sensorineural loss on the right.
options: A sensorineural loss on the right
A conductive loss on the left
A conductive loss on the right
A sensorineural loss on the left
cards.explanation: Normal Rinne results on both sides mean no middle ear block anywhere, so a lateralizing Weber must reflect a difference between the two cochleas, and the tone is heard on the better side. Hearing it on the left therefore places the damage on the right. Naming the side the tone is heard in is the most common recording error on this test. Either conductive answer would require a reversed Rinne, which was not found.

cards.q: A subject stands steadily with the eyes open but sways markedly and has to step out when the eyes close. How is this Romberg result interpreted?
cards.a: Positive, indicating that vision was compensating for a balance deficit.
options: Negative, since the subject was steady with the eyes open
Positive, indicating that vision was compensating for a balance deficit
Positive, indicating weakness of the leg muscles
Invalid, because the arms were at the sides rather than held outstretched
cards.explanation: The whole design of the test rests on the comparison between the two conditions, so steadiness with vision followed by instability without it is the positive finding and points to the non visual balance channels. Calling it negative uses only half of the observation. Muscle weakness would show up with the eyes open as well, and arms at the sides is the standard position rather than a protocol violation.

cards.q: On the Rinne test the tone fades at the mastoid and the subject then hears it again when the fork is moved beside the ear canal. How is this recorded and what does it mean?
cards.a: Air conduction greater than bone conduction, which is the normal pattern.
options: Bone conduction greater than air conduction, indicating a conductive loss
Air conduction greater than bone conduction, indicating a sensorineural loss
Air conduction greater than bone conduction, which is the normal pattern
An inconclusive result requiring a different fork
cards.explanation: Hearing the tone return by the air route after it has faded through bone shows the middle ear is amplifying as it should, which is the expected finding in a healthy ear. The reverse pattern, where nothing is heard at the ear canal after the mastoid tone fades, is what flags a conductive block. A normal Rinne does not by itself prove hearing is normal, because a sensorineural loss preserves this ordering while raising both thresholds, so it must be read with the Weber.

cards.q: A student is spun ten times to the right in a rotating chair and then stopped. What is observed immediately afterward?
cards.a: A sensation of turning to the left, with nystagmus whose quick phase beats to the left.
options: A sensation of turning to the left, with nystagmus whose quick phase beats to the left
A sensation of turning to the right, with nystagmus whose quick phase beats to the right
No sensation and no eye movement, since the rotation has stopped
A sensation of falling backward, with the eyes fixed straight ahead
cards.explanation: During the spin the endolymph came up to speed with the canal, so when the head stops the fluid keeps moving and deflects the cupula the opposite way, which the brain reads as rotation in the reverse direction and which drives the eyes accordingly. That is why the post rotatory response reverses instead of matching the original spin. Stopping does not switch the system off, and the illusion is rotational rather than a sense of falling.

cards.q: A subject has cerumen fully occluding the left ear canal. Predict both tuning fork results before the wax is removed.
cards.a: Weber lateralizes to the left, and the left Rinne shows bone conduction outlasting air conduction.
options: Weber lateralizes to the right, and the left Rinne shows bone outlasting air conduction
Weber lateralizes to the left, and both ears show air outlasting bone conduction
Weber lateralizes to the left, and the left Rinne shows bone conduction outlasting air conduction
Weber stays midline, and the left Rinne shows air outlasting bone conduction
cards.explanation: A blocked canal stops airborne sound from reaching an otherwise healthy ear, so this is a conductive loss and both tests should say so: the Rinne reverses on the blocked side because bone conduction bypasses the plug, and the Weber goes toward the blocked ear because that cochlea is intact and shielded from room noise. Sending the Weber to the right would indicate a damaged left cochlea instead. A preserved Rinne on the left would mean the canal was not truly blocked.

cards.q: A subject is steady on the Romberg with eyes open and closed but shows no nystagmus at all after ten rotations in the chair. What do these two results together suggest?
cards.a: Canal function is impaired, while vision and proprioception keep the subject upright.
options: Both the vestibular system and proprioception have failed, since the chair test was negative
Canal function is impaired, while vision and proprioception keep the subject upright
The cochlea is damaged bilaterally, which explains the absent nystagmus
The results are normal, since a steady Romberg rules out any vestibular problem
cards.explanation: Post rotatory nystagmus is a direct readout of the canals, so its absence points to a vestibular problem, while quiet standing can be maintained on proprioception alone, which is why the Romberg can look normal in the same person. Reading the two tests together is what makes the pattern interpretable. A failure of proprioception as well would have produced swaying with the eyes closed, and the cochlea handles hearing rather than eye movements.

cards.q: A subject reports the Weber tone as louder on the right. Before recording a diagnosis, which single follow up best distinguishes the two possible causes?
cards.a: Perform the Rinne on the right ear and compare bone with air conduction.
options: Repeat the Weber with the fork on the left mastoid instead
Ask the subject to plug the right ear and repeat the Weber test on the forehead
Perform the Rinne on the right ear and compare bone with air conduction
Test the left ear with a lower frequency fork
cards.explanation: Lateralization to the right is ambiguous on its own, because it fits either a right conductive block or a left sensorineural loss, and only a comparison of the two delivery routes settles which. A reversed Rinne on the right confirms the conductive explanation, and a normal one shifts the diagnosis to the opposite ear. Moving the fork off the midline abandons the equal stimulus the Weber depends on, plugging an ear adds an artificial block on top of the finding, and changing the fork frequency does not address the question.

cards.q: A classmate insists that a normal Rinne in both ears proves a subject hears normally. Using the logic of the two tests, what is the best response?
cards.a: A sensorineural loss keeps air over bone, so the Rinne can be normal despite loss.
options: A conductive loss also preserves the air over bone ordering, so the Rinne misses it
The Rinne is unreliable at 512 Hz, so it should be repeated at a lower frequency
A sensorineural loss keeps air over bone, so the Rinne can be normal despite loss
The Rinne measures loudness rather than conduction, so it says nothing about hearing
cards.explanation: The Rinne asks only whether the middle ear is doing its amplifying job, so when the cochlea is damaged the two routes are both reduced and their normal ordering survives, which is exactly why the Weber is done alongside it. Tuning fork tests screen for the type of loss rather than measure thresholds, and an audiogram is what quantifies hearing. Conductive loss is the one thing the Rinne detects well, and the standard 512 Hz fork is appropriate for the test.
